01_A_particle_model_for_solids_liquids_a.title: A particle model for solids, liquids and gases
01_A_particle_model_for_solids_liquids_a.subject: Chemistry

objectives.statement: Distinguish solids, liquids and gases by their shape, their volume and whether they flow.
Describe the particle spacing, arrangement and motion of a solid, a liquid and a gas using the kinetic particle model.
Use the particle model to explain the shape, volume and relative compressibility of each state, without changing the identity or the size of the particles.

prerequisites.statement: Distinguish a material from the container that holds it (for example, water is not the same thing as the glass holding it).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The particle model explains a substance's own shape and volume, not the shape of whatever happens to be holding it at the time.

prerequisites.statement: Read a numbered volume scale, such as the markings on a syringe or a measuring cylinder, in cm³.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Several activities in this lesson compare the volume of air or water read directly from a syringe.

diagnostic_items.question: Water is poured from a tall, narrow glass into a wide, shallow dish. Has the volume of the water changed?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: No. The water's volume stays the same; only its shape changes, because it now takes the shape of the dish instead of the glass.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Yes, it has less volume now because the water looks shallower.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner judges volume from the apparent height of the liquid rather than recognising that the same amount of water has simply spread out.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks whether the learner already separates a liquid's own volume from the shape of its container, before the particle model is used to explain why.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Pour the same small volume of water into two very different containers side by side and ask what has and has not changed.

diagnostic_items.question: A gas-tight syringe has a scale marked in cm³. The front edge of the plunger sits exactly on the 35 cm³ mark. What volume of air is in the syringe?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: 35 cm³, read directly from the scale at the plunger's position.

common_wrong_answers.answer: It cannot be known without knowing the syringe's total capacity.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner does not yet trust a direct scale reading as a complete answer on its own.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks that the learner can read a volume scale directly before volumes are compared across the three states.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Practise reading two or three further syringe positions aloud before using any numbers in the lesson.

theory_blocks.title: Three materials, three behaviours
theory_blocks.body:
A wooden block keeps its shape and its size however it is placed down. Water poured from a glass into a dish keeps the same amount but spreads out to match the dish. Air pushed into a balloon has no shape or volume of its own at all: it simply occupies whatever space is available to it.

These three behaviours are observations, not definitions of three different kinds of particle. The same explanation has to work for the block, the water and the air, and it has to predict what would happen to a new material you have never seen before. That explanation is the kinetic particle model: [[blue:particles that do not change their identity, only their spacing, arrangement and motion]].

theory_blocks.title: The kinetic particle model

assets.caption: The same particle, drawn the same size in all three states: closely packed and regularly arranged in a solid, closely packed but disordered in a liquid, and far apart in a gas. The short double-headed arrows show solid particles vibrating about fixed positions; the curved arrows show liquid particles moving around one another, and the straight arrows show gas particles travelling freely in all directions. The liquid takes the shape of the lower part of a taller container; the gas spreads to fill a much bigger one.
assets.purpose: Make spacing, arrangement and motion directly comparable across the three states using one consistent symbol.

theory_blocks.body:
In a **solid**, particles are packed closely together, usually in a regular, repeating arrangement, and each one vibrates about a fixed position without travelling past its neighbours. In a **liquid**, particles are still close together, but the regular arrangement is lost: particles are free to move around one another, which is why a liquid flows and takes the shape of the lower part of its container. In a **gas**, particles are much farther apart than in a solid or liquid, and they move freely and randomly in all directions, colliding with each other and with the walls of the container.

The figure draws exactly the same particle symbol, at the same size, in each state. Only three things change between the states: how far apart the particles are, how they are arranged, and how they move. Nothing about the particle itself changes.

theory_blocks.title: Why a gas squashes easily and a liquid almost doesn't
theory_blocks.body:
Compressing a sample means pushing its particles closer together. In a gas, most of the volume is empty space between particles that are far apart, so there is a great deal of space to remove: a gas is readily compressed. In a liquid, the particles are already almost as close together as they can get without becoming a solid, so pushing them even closer is very difficult: a liquid's volume changes only very slightly under the pressures used in an ordinary classroom. A solid's particles are held in fixed positions by strong attractions and are even harder to push together.

It is tempting to group liquids and gases together because both flow and neither keeps a fixed shape. For compressibility, though, the liquid behaves much more like the solid than like the gas: **close-packed particles (solid and liquid) resist compression; widely spaced particles (gas) do not.**

theory_blocks.title: What the diagram shows, and what it never claims
theory_blocks.body: A particle diagram is deliberately simplified. The circles show spacing and motion; they are not a photograph of the real shape, colour or size of a molecule. Three claims the model does **not** make: [[blue:a solid's particles are not frozen (they vibrate continuously)]]; [[orange:a gas particle does not swell up when the gas expands (the same small particles simply spread further apart)]]; and [[teal:a substance does not become a different substance when it changes state (the same particles are rearranged, not replaced)]]. Whenever the same substance is drawn in more than one state, the same particle symbol, at the same size, should appear in every drawing.

keywords.definition: The model that explains the properties of solids, liquids and gases in terms of particle spacing, arrangement and motion.
How easily a sample's volume can be reduced by squeezing it; it depends on how much empty space there is between the particles.
One of the three physical forms — solid, liquid or gas — that a substance can exist in.

worked_examples.statement: **Classifying an unfamiliar sample.** A sealed, rigid plastic bottle contains a sample that keeps a fixed shape and a fixed volume however the bottle is turned. State which of the three states the sample is in, and describe its particle spacing, arrangement and motion.
knowns: The sample keeps both a fixed shape and a fixed volume regardless of orientation.
unknowns: The state of the sample and its particle description.
worked_examples.solution: A fixed shape together with a fixed volume is the defining pair of properties of a solid: a liquid would take the shape of the lower part of the bottle, and a gas would have no shape of its own. The sample's particles are therefore closely packed in a regular arrangement, and each particle vibrates about a fixed position rather than moving past its neighbours.
worked_examples.interpretation: Both stated properties (fixed shape AND fixed volume) point to the same state, which is a useful check: a single property is sometimes ambiguous, but shape and volume together identify a solid uniquely among the three states.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Concluding 'liquid' from 'it can be poured out when the lid is removed' — pourability is a property of the container being opened, not of the undisturbed sample described in the question.

worked_examples.statement: **Reading a particle diagram.** A diagram shows particles spread far apart, moving freely in random directions and colliding with the walls of a large, closed container. Identify the state shown and predict what happens to the volume of this sample if it is squeezed into a much smaller, sealed container at a similar temperature.
knowns: Particles are far apart.
Motion is free and random in all directions.
The container is sealed.
unknowns: The state of the sample and its response to compression.
worked_examples.solution: Wide particle spacing together with free, random motion is the gas description, not the solid or liquid description. A gas is readily compressed because most of its volume is empty space between particles. Squeezing it into a smaller sealed container reduces the average distance between the same particles; the particles themselves do not shrink, and none escape because the container stays sealed.
worked_examples.interpretation: The sample still contains exactly as many particles as before; only the spacing between them has decreased, which is consistent with the kinetic particle model and not with particles disappearing or shrinking.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Saying the particles 'get squashed' or 'get smaller' — compression changes the spacing between particles, never the size of a particle.

worked_examples.statement: **Explaining a spreading gas.** A small amount of gas released into a large, empty room spreads out until it has filled the whole room. Explain, using the particle model, why this happens without any of the gas particles growing in size.
knowns: A fixed, small number of gas particles.
They end up spread through a much larger volume (the room) than their starting container.
unknowns: How the same particles can occupy so much more space.
reasoning: Gas particles move freely and randomly in all directions, not along one fixed path.
With no walls close by in most directions, particles that happen to move away from the release point keep travelling until they meet a wall of the room.
Given enough time, random motion in all directions spreads the fixed number of particles throughout the whole available volume, because there is nothing holding them back from doing so.
The particles that end up near the far side of the room are the very same particles that started near the release point: none of them have grown, and no new particles have appeared.
worked_examples.solution: The gas fills the room because its particles move freely and randomly in every direction and are not held together by strong attractions, so with enough time they spread until they occupy the whole available space. The particle count and particle size are unchanged throughout; only the average spacing between particles has increased.
worked_examples.interpretation: This is the key reasoning of the lesson: a larger occupied volume is explained by spacing between an unchanged number of unchanged particles, never by particles themselves expanding.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Describing the spreading as the gas being 'pushed' into the room by some external force — in this scenario nothing pushes the gas; its own particles' random motion is sufficient.

guided_exercises.statement: A sample flows to take up the lower part of whatever container it is placed in, but a fixed amount of it always occupies the same total space. Name the state, and describe its particle spacing, arrangement and motion.
hints: Decide first whether the sample has a fixed shape, a fixed volume, both, or neither.
A fixed volume but a changing shape rules out two of the three states.
Match your answer to the particle description used for that state earlier in the lesson.
guided_exercises.answer: The sample is a liquid: a fixed volume but a shape that follows the container is the defining pair of liquid properties.
guided_exercises.full_solution: Particles in this liquid are close together, as in a solid, but their arrangement is disordered rather than regular, and they are free to move around one another. This mobility is what lets the sample flow into the shape of its container while the total space it occupies (set by how many particles there are and how closely they are packed) stays the same.
common_errors: Choosing 'gas' because the sample flows — flowing is shared by liquids and gases, but only a gas also lacks a fixed volume; this sample keeps a fixed volume, so it is a liquid.

guided_exercises.statement: Two identical, sealed syringes are set up: one holds 50 cm³ of air, the other holds 50 cm³ of water. A similar pushing force is applied to each plunger. Predict and explain which syringe's content changes volume more.
hints: Compare how closely packed the particles already are in each sample before pushing.
More empty space between particles means more room for that space to be removed.
State your answer as a comparison, not just a description of one syringe.
guided_exercises.answer: The air (gas) sample's volume decreases far more than the water (liquid) sample's volume.
guided_exercises.full_solution: Air particles are widely spaced, so a large fraction of the syringe's volume is empty space between them; pushing the plunger removes much of that space, so the volume falls noticeably. Water particles are already packed almost as closely as they can get, so there is very little space left to remove, and the water's volume barely changes for the same push.
common_errors: Predicting similar behaviour for both because 'liquids and gases both flow' — flowing and compressibility are different properties, and liquids pattern with solids, not gases, for compressibility.

exercises.statement: A sealed syringe contains 60 cm³ of air. The plunger is pushed in until the air occupies 20 cm³, with no air escaping. Calculate the fraction by which the volume has decreased, and explain in particle terms why this large a decrease is possible for air but would not be possible for an equal starting volume of water.
exercises.answer: The volume has decreased by two-thirds ($\frac{60-20}{60}=\frac{40}{60}=\frac{2}{3}$, about 66.7%).
exercises.full_solution: $\dfrac{60\,\mathrm{cm^3}-20\,\mathrm{cm^3}}{60\,\mathrm{cm^3}}=\dfrac{40}{60}=\dfrac{2}{3}\approx 66.7\%$. This large a decrease is possible because air particles start far apart, so most of the original 60 cm³ is empty space that can be removed by pushing the plunger. An equal 60 cm³ sample of water has particles already packed almost as closely as possible, so pushing the plunger with the same force would reduce its volume by only a small fraction.
common_errors: Calculating $\frac{20}{60}$ instead of the fractional decrease $\frac{40}{60}$ — the question asks how much the volume has fallen BY, not what fraction of the original volume remains.

exercises.statement: For each sample below, name the state (solid, liquid or gas) and give the particle spacing, arrangement and motion that explains it: (a) a metal nail that keeps its shape when moved; (b) cooking oil that takes the shape of the bottom of any pan it is poured into, while the same amount always fills the same depth in a given pan; (c) the air inside a fully inflated car tyre.
exercises.answer: (a) solid; (b) liquid; (c) gas.
exercises.full_solution: (a) The nail keeps a fixed shape and volume: particles are closely packed in a regular arrangement, vibrating about fixed positions. (b) The oil keeps a fixed volume but takes the shape of its container: particles are closely packed but disordered, moving around one another. (c) The air in the tyre has no shape or volume of its own and fills the whole tyre: particles are far apart, moving freely and randomly, colliding with each other and the tyre wall.

exercises.statement: A student draws a gas as a few large circles with blank space between them, each circle far bigger than the particles they drew earlier for the same substance as a solid. Identify what is scientifically wrong with this gas diagram and redraw it correctly in words.
exercises.answer: The particles are drawn too large: the same substance must use the same-sized particle symbol in every state.
exercises.full_solution: The diagram wrongly suggests that particles grow when a substance becomes a gas. A correct diagram keeps the circles the same size as in the solid drawing, but spaces them much farther apart and adds arrows showing free, random motion in all directions; the empty space between particles increases, not the size of the particles themselves.

exam_questions.statement: A sealed cylinder contains a gas. Explain, using ideas about particles, why this gas can be compressed into a much smaller volume far more easily than an equal volume of liquid in an identical sealed cylinder.
exam_questions.answer: Gas particles are far apart with a great deal of empty space between them, so pushing them closer together removes mostly empty space and allows a large volume decrease; liquid particles are already packed almost as closely as possible, leaving very little space to remove, so the liquid's volume changes only slightly for the same compression.
mark_scheme: States that gas particles are far apart / widely spaced.
States that there is a large amount of empty space between gas particles that can be removed.
States that liquid particles are already close together (comparable to a solid).
Links the small amount of space between liquid particles to only a small possible volume change.

challenge_questions.statement:
Diagrams A, B and C below are all meant to show the **same pure substance**, each in a different state, drawn in three identical containers.

(a) Name the state that each diagram is meant to show, and give the particle spacing, arrangement and motion that goes with it.

(b) One of the three diagrams cannot be a correct drawing of the same substance as the other two. Identify it and explain what is wrong with it.

(c) Describe in words how you would redraw that diagram correctly.
challenge_questions.answer: (a) A is the solid, B is the gas and C is the liquid. (b) B is wrong: its circles are drawn far larger than the circles in A and C, so it suggests that each particle grows when the substance becomes a gas. (c) Redraw B with circles exactly the same size as those in A and C, spread far apart throughout the whole container, with straight arrows pointing in different directions to show free, random motion.
challenge_questions.full_solution:
(a) A shows particles that are closely packed in a regular, repeating arrangement; each one vibrates about a fixed position, so A is the solid. C shows particles that are just as closely packed but disordered, and they occupy only the lower part of the container; they move around one another, so C is the liquid. B shows particles that are far apart with a great deal of empty space between them, moving freely and randomly, so B is the gas.

(b) Changing state never changes what a particle is or how big it is — only the spacing, the arrangement and the motion. B therefore cannot show the same substance as A and C, because its circles are roughly one and a half times the diameter of the circles in A and C. Wide spacing on its own is correct for a gas; the oversized circles are not.

(c) A correct gas diagram for this substance uses the same circle size as A and C. The circles are spread far apart so that most of the container is empty space, and short straight arrows in several different directions show that the particles travel freely and randomly, colliding with each other and with the container walls.

assets.caption: Three identical containers holding the same pure substance in three different states. A: closely packed, regular. B: far apart, but the circles are drawn much larger than in A and C. C: closely packed, disordered, occupying the lower part of the container.
assets.purpose: Give the student a particle diagram to read and correct, as C1.1.2 and P2.1.2 require.

challenge_questions.statement:
A sealed, rigid glass tube contains a small amount of one pure substance as a solid. The tube is warmed gently until all of the solid has become a liquid. The mass of the sealed tube and its contents is measured before the warming and again afterwards, and the two readings are identical.

(a) State what has changed about the particles inside the tube, and what has not changed.

(b) Explain why the mass reading is unchanged, even though the contents now look completely different.

(c) A student says that the liquid is 'a new substance that the heating made'. Use the evidence in this experiment to explain why the student is wrong.
challenge_questions.answer: (a) The arrangement, the spacing and the motion of the particles have changed; the particles themselves — how many there are, how big they are and what they are — have not changed. (b) The tube is sealed, so no particles can enter or leave, and none are created or destroyed; the same particles are still inside, so the total mass is the same. (c) A new substance would have to be made of different particles. The identical mass in a sealed tube shows that exactly the same particles are still present, just arranged and moving differently, so no new substance has been made.
challenge_questions.full_solution:
(a) In the solid, the particles were closely packed in a regular arrangement, each vibrating about a fixed position. In the liquid, the same particles are still close together but the regular arrangement has been lost, and they now move around one another. Their number, their size and their identity are the same before and after.

(b) Mass depends on how many particles there are and what they are, not on how they are arranged. Because the tube is sealed, nothing can escape and nothing can get in, so the balance reading cannot change. A change in mass would be a sign that something had been lost or gained, and nothing has been.

(c) The student is describing a change of substance, but the evidence shows a change of state. The mass is identical, the tube is sealed, and no new material has appeared or disappeared; the only differences are in particle arrangement, spacing and motion. The same particles that made the solid now make the liquid, so it is the same substance in a different state.

mcq.stem: A small amount of gas released in one corner of a sealed, empty room eventually fills the whole room. What best explains this, using the particle model?

options.text: The same number of gas particles move freely and randomly in all directions and spread out until they occupy the whole available space.
Each gas particle expands in size until the particles together take up the whole room.
options.why_wrong: particles do not change size when a gas expands; only the spacing between an unchanged number of particles increases.

options.text: New gas particles are continuously created to fill the empty space in the room.
options.why_wrong: no new particles are created; the room is sealed and the same fixed number of particles simply spreads out.

options.text: The room's air pushes the gas particles into every corner.
options.why_wrong: the spreading is explained by the gas particles' own random motion, not by being pushed by something else in the room.

mcq.explanation: a fixed number of unchanged particles, moving freely and randomly, spreads through the whole available volume given enough time; nothing about an individual particle changes.

mcq.stem: Equal sealed samples of water and air are each squeezed with a similar force. Which statement correctly compares their volume changes?

options.text: The water's volume decreases far more than the air's, because liquids flow more easily than gases.
options.why_wrong: flowing easily is not the same property as being easy to compress; this reverses which state compresses more.

options.text: The air's volume decreases far more than the water's, because air particles start much farther apart and have far more removable space between them.
Both decrease in volume by a similar amount, because both water and air are fluids that take the shape of their container.
options.why_wrong: sharing the property of flowing does not mean two states share the property of compressibility; their particle spacing is very different.

options.text: Neither changes in volume, because particles cannot be pushed closer together once a container is sealed.
options.why_wrong: sealing a container prevents particles escaping, not particles moving closer together; compression still changes spacing inside a sealed container.

mcq.explanation: air's widely spaced particles leave much more removable space than water's already closely packed particles, so air compresses far more for the same applied force.

mcq.stem: A particle diagram shows particles packed closely together but in a disordered arrangement, free to move around one another. Which state does this diagram represent?

options.text: Solid
options.why_wrong: a solid's particles are in a regular, repeating arrangement and vibrate about fixed positions rather than moving around one another.

options.text: Gas
options.why_wrong: a gas's particles are far apart, not closely packed.

options.text: Liquid
It could be any of the three states, since all particles move.
options.why_wrong: close packing together with a disordered arrangement and particles moving around one another is specific to a liquid; it does not match a solid's fixed positions or a gas's wide spacing.

mcq.explanation: close packing with a disordered arrangement and particles free to move around one another is the liquid description, distinct from the solid's regular packing and the gas's wide spacing.

flashcards.front: What does the kinetic particle model use to explain the three states of matter?
flashcards.back: The spacing, arrangement and motion of particles — not any change in what the particles are.

flashcards.front: How does particle spacing in a liquid compare with a solid and with a gas?
flashcards.back: A liquid's particles are about as close together as a solid's, but disordered rather than regularly arranged; a gas's particles are much farther apart than both.

flashcards.front: True or false: the particles in a solid are completely still.
flashcards.back: False. Solid particles vibrate continuously about fixed positions; they are never completely still.

flashcards.front: Which state has no fixed shape and no fixed volume?
flashcards.back: A gas: it spreads to fill whatever space is available to it.

flashcards.front: Why is a gas much easier to compress than a liquid?
flashcards.back: A gas's particles are far apart, so most of its volume is removable empty space; a liquid's particles are already packed almost as closely as possible, leaving very little space to remove.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The particles in a solid are completely still.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: A solid object looks and feels motionless, so learners extend that stillness down to the particle scale.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner describes solid particles as 'frozen in place' or draws them with no motion at all.
misconceptions.correct_model: Solid particles vibrate about fixed positions; they do not travel past one another, but they are never completely still.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask what would happen to the vibration if the solid were heated, without yet melting it, and connect faster vibration to a warmer solid.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: An individual gas particle swells up until it fills the whole container.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Learners see a gas filling a balloon or a room and attribute the expansion to the particles themselves growing, rather than to particles spreading apart.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner draws one enormous gas particle, or says the particles 'get bigger' when a gas expands.
misconceptions.correct_model: A fixed number of unchanged, small particles simply spread out so that the average distance between them increases; the container looks full because the particles are moving throughout the whole space, not because any particle has grown.
misconceptions.remediation: Compare the same number of counters in a small box and a large box: the counters are identical in size in both cases, only their spacing changes.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A liquid can be squashed into a smaller volume about as easily as a gas.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Textbooks sometimes group liquids and gases together as 'able to flow' or 'not keeping a fixed shape', which can be over-read as meaning they behave alike under pressure too.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner predicts that pressing on a sealed syringe of water will noticeably reduce its volume, in the same way as pressing on a syringe of air.
misconceptions.correct_model: A gas is readily compressed because its particles are widely separated and there is a lot of empty space between them to remove. A liquid's particles are already packed almost as closely as a solid's, so pressing on a liquid changes its volume only very slightly under ordinary classroom pressures.
misconceptions.remediation: Compare a sealed syringe of air and a sealed syringe of water side by side when the plunger of each is pushed with similar force.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: When a substance changes state, it becomes a different substance.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Melting ice looks like a completely different material from solid ice, so learners sometimes treat the change as if the identity of the substance itself has changed.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner says water 'turns into something else' when it melts or boils, rather than describing a change in the arrangement of the same particles.
misconceptions.correct_model: A change of state rearranges the spacing, arrangement and motion of the same particles; it does not change what the particles are. Ice, liquid water and steam are all made of the same water particles.
misconceptions.remediation: Draw the same labelled particle as solid, liquid and gas, and ask the learner to point to what has and has not changed between the three drawings.

common_mistakes.mistake: Drawing gas particles much larger than the same substance's solid particles.
common_mistakes.why: This wrongly suggests that particles swell when a substance becomes a gas.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always use the same particle symbol at the same size in every state of the same substance; only spacing, arrangement and motion change.

common_mistakes.mistake: Describing solid particles as completely motionless.
common_mistakes.why: A solid object looks still from the outside, so the stillness is wrongly extended down to the particle scale.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Remember that solid particles vibrate continuously about fixed positions; only their ability to travel past neighbours is removed, not all motion.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating liquids and gases as equally compressible because both flow.
common_mistakes.why: Flowing and being easy to compress are different properties that happen to coincide for a gas but not for a liquid.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Judge compressibility from particle spacing, not from whether a sample flows: close packing (solid and liquid) resists compression; wide spacing (gas) does not.

common_mistakes.mistake: Saying a substance becomes 'something else' when it changes state.
common_mistakes.why: A melted or boiled substance can look very different from its starting state, which invites the idea that it has become a different material.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Track the same labelled particle through solid, liquid and gas drawings and point out what has and has not changed between them.

exam_notes: When asked to 'describe' a state, give spacing, arrangement AND motion — a one-word answer such as 'close together' rarely earns full marks.
When comparing compressibility, name BOTH states being compared and the reason for the difference; a bare 'gases compress more' without a particle reason is incomplete.
Never write that a particle 'gets bigger', 'gets smaller' or 'becomes a different particle' during any physical change — spacing and arrangement change; particle identity and size never do.
A question about a container with a specific shape and volume is testing whether you can infer the state from BOTH properties together, not from either alone.

summary.big_idea: The same particles, unchanged in identity and size, explain all three states and their properties through differences in spacing, arrangement and motion alone.
key_points: A solid keeps a fixed shape and volume: particles are closely packed, regularly arranged and vibrate about fixed positions.
A liquid keeps a fixed volume but takes the shape of its container: particles are closely packed but disordered and move around one another.
A gas has no fixed shape or volume: particles are far apart and move freely and randomly, filling the available space.
A gas compresses easily because there is a great deal of removable empty space between its particles; a liquid barely compresses because its particles are already closely packed.
Changing state rearranges spacing, arrangement and motion only — the particles themselves never change identity or size.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Same particles, same size, every time — only their spacing, arrangement and motion change between solid, liquid and gas.

objectives.statement: Describe melting, boiling, evaporating, freezing and condensing, and identify the direction of particle-spacing change in each.
Explain, using particle energy and attractions, why a substance changes state and why a pure substance's temperature stays constant during the change.
Distinguish evaporation at a liquid's surface from boiling throughout the liquid, and state that the substance remains the same substance throughout any change of state.

prerequisites.statement: The kinetic particle model: particle spacing, arrangement and motion distinguish solids, liquids and gases.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every change of state in this lesson is described as a change in exactly these three things, for the same unchanged particles.

prerequisites.statement: Temperature is a measure of how energetically particles move, on average: a higher temperature means more energetic average motion.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The energy explanation for melting, boiling, freezing and condensing depends on linking heating and cooling to particle energy, not only to a number on a thermometer.

diagnostic_items.question: Sample A is heated steadily and sample B is cooled steadily, both starting at the same temperature. In which sample are the particles moving more energetically, on average, after this?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: Sample A. Heating increases the average energy of particle motion, so A's particles end up moving more energetically than B's, whose particles have lost energy by cooling.

common_wrong_answers.answer: They end up the same, because they started at the same temperature.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner answers from the starting condition and does not yet connect heating/cooling to a change in particle energy.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks that heating and cooling are already linked to particle energy, before that link is used to explain every change of state in this lesson.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Revisit the solid/liquid/gas motion descriptions from the previous lesson and ask what heating would do to the speed of vibration or movement in each.

theory_blocks.title: Five named changes, one reversible picture

assets.caption: The five changes of state as a reversible cycle between the same three states. Each arrow names one process: the upper arrows (heating) increase particle spacing, and the lower arrows (cooling) decrease it.
assets.purpose: Show that all five processes are the same few transitions, named by direction, rather than five unrelated pieces of vocabulary to memorise separately.

theory_blocks.body:
**Melting** is solid to liquid; **freezing** is liquid to solid, the exact reverse. **Boiling** and **evaporating** are both liquid to gas; **condensing** is gas to liquid, the reverse of both. Every one of these five names describes a direction between the same three states, for the same substance.

[[orange:Heating]] drives the changes that increase particle spacing (melting, boiling, evaporating); [[blue:cooling]] drives the changes that decrease it (freezing, condensing). Each change is a physical change only: the substance is exactly the same substance before and after.

theory_blocks.title: Telling evaporation and boiling apart
theory_blocks.body:
Three questions separate the two processes. *Where does it happen?* Evaporation happens only at the liquid's exposed surface; boiling happens throughout the whole liquid, with bubbles of vapour forming inside it. *At what temperature?* Evaporation can happen at any temperature at which the substance is a liquid, including well below the boiling point; boiling happens only once the liquid reaches its boiling point at the surrounding pressure. *How fast and how visibly?* Evaporation is usually slow and produces no bubbles; boiling is rapid once started and is visibly bubbling throughout the liquid.

A puddle drying on a warm day, well below 100°C, is evaporation. Water bubbling throughout a pan on a stove at 100°C is boiling.

theory_blocks.title: What never changes during a change of state
theory_blocks.body: None of the five changes of state create, destroy or convert a particle into a different kind of particle: they rearrange the same particles' spacing, arrangement and motion. [[blue:Cooling never works by removing particles from a sample; it removes energy from the particles that are already there]], and the same number of particles ends up moving less energetically (and, often, more closely packed) than before.

theory_blocks.title: Where the energy goes during a change of state
theory_blocks.body:
While a substance stays in one state, heating increases the average energy of particle motion and its temperature rises. During melting or boiling of a pure substance, energy continues to enter the substance, but that energy is used to let particles overcome enough of the attraction holding them in place to rearrange or separate — not to speed up their average motion further. This is why temperature stays constant for as long as the change of state is still happening (the full graph of this behaviour is the subject of the next lesson).

Attraction between particles is never switched off by this process. In a liquid, significant attraction remains; it is simply no longer enough to hold particles in fixed positions, as it was in the solid. Freezing and condensing reverse the energy flow: energy leaves the substance as its particles lose enough energy for attraction to pull them back into a liquid's close, mobile arrangement or a solid's fixed, ordered one.

keywords.definition: The change of state from solid to liquid.
The change of state from liquid to gas, occurring throughout the liquid at its boiling point.
The change of state from liquid to gas, occurring only at the liquid's surface and possible at any temperature below the boiling point.
The change of state from gas to liquid.
The change of state from liquid to solid.

worked_examples.statement: **Naming the change.** Overnight, water vapour in the air touches a cold window and forms liquid droplets on the inside of the glass. Name this change of state and state the direction of particle-spacing change involved.
knowns: Water starts as a gas (vapour) in the air.
Water ends as a liquid (droplets) on the glass.
unknowns: The name of the change and its spacing direction.
worked_examples.solution: Gas to liquid is the direction described. The name for gas to liquid is condensation. Particle spacing decreases: the widely spaced gas particles end up close together as a liquid.
worked_examples.interpretation: The same water particles that were spread through the air end up packed closely together as droplets; none have been created or destroyed.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Naming this 'freezing' — freezing is liquid to solid, not gas to liquid; the window droplets are still liquid water, not ice.

worked_examples.statement: **Evaporation or boiling?** A wet pavement dries out over the course of a warm afternoon with the air at about 25°C. Decide whether this is evaporation or boiling, and justify the choice using the three distinguishing questions from the lesson.
knowns: The water disappears gradually over hours.
The air temperature (about 25°C) is far below water's boiling point (100°C).
worked_examples.solution: Where: the water loss happens only at the exposed surface of the puddle, not throughout its depth. Temperature: 25°C is well below water's boiling point of 100°C. Speed/visibility: the process is slow, with no bubbles seen at any point. All three answers point to evaporation, not boiling.
worked_examples.interpretation: Every one of the three distinguishing questions gives the same answer, which is a useful check: a genuine ambiguity would show up as the three questions pointing in different directions.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Concluding 'boiling' simply because the liquid is disappearing — boiling is one specific process for turning liquid into gas, not a synonym for 'losing liquid to the air'.

worked_examples.statement: **Why the temperature does not rise.** A beaker of ice at 0°C is heated at a slow, steady rate. For several minutes, the thermometer reading stays at exactly 0°C even though the heater keeps supplying energy. Explain why, in terms of particle energy and attraction.
knowns: Energy is being supplied continuously.
The temperature reading does not change while ice and liquid water coexist.
unknowns: Where the supplied energy is going, if not into raising temperature.
reasoning: Temperature reflects the average energy of particle motion, so a constant temperature means that average motion energy is not increasing during this stage.
The supplied energy is instead being used to let particles overcome enough of the attraction holding them in the solid's fixed, ordered positions.

Once a particle has enough energy to break free of its fixed position and join the liquid's disordered, mobile arrangement, it has used that portion of the supplied energy for rearrangement, not for extra motion energy.

Only once melting is complete, with no solid left to rearrange, does further supplied energy go back into increasing the average motion energy of the (now entirely liquid) particles, and the temperature starts rising again.
worked_examples.solution: The energy supplied during melting is used to let particles overcome enough of the attraction holding them in fixed positions so they can rearrange into the liquid's disordered, mobile structure, rather than to increase their average motion energy. Since temperature measures that average motion energy, it stays constant until melting is complete.
worked_examples.interpretation: This is the precise, GCSE-level replacement for a common textbook's looser phrase about attraction 'weakening': attraction is overcome enough for rearrangement, but real attraction remains in the liquid that follows.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Saying 'the heater must have stopped working' — the heater is still supplying energy throughout; it is the destination of that energy that changes, not its presence.

worked_examples.statement: **Exam-style: explain and distinguish.** 'A pan of water is heated on a stove. Before it reaches 100°C, steam can already be seen rising gently from the surface. Once it reaches 100°C, bubbles form throughout the water and it boils vigorously.' Explain both observations using ideas from this lesson.
knowns: Gentle rising vapour is seen before 100°C.
Vigorous bubbling throughout the water starts at 100°C.
unknowns: The name and mechanism behind each observation.
worked_examples.solution: The gentle rising vapour before 100°C is evaporation: particles at the exposed surface that happen to have enough energy escape into the air, even though the bulk of the liquid is below the boiling point. At 100°C, the water has reached its boiling point at normal atmospheric pressure, so particles throughout the liquid (not only at the surface) now have enough energy to overcome the attraction holding them in the liquid and form bubbles of vapour, which is boiling. The identity of the substance is the same water throughout both stages; only the location, rate and temperature condition of the liquid-to-gas change differ. (Strictly, water vapour itself is invisible: the 'steam' you can see is a mist of tiny droplets formed when some of that escaping vapour condenses in the cooler air just above the pan.)
worked_examples.interpretation: A single exam scenario often asks for both processes in one answer: structuring the response as 'before 100°C: evaporation, because…' and 'at 100°C: boiling, because…' addresses both parts clearly.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Describing the early vapour as 'the water starting to boil early' — boiling is defined as happening at the boiling point throughout the liquid; vapour appearing earlier, only at the surface, is evaporation by definition.

guided_exercises.statement: A candle is burning. Solid wax close to the flame turns into a pool of liquid wax at the top of the candle, and liquid wax that runs down the cooler side of the candle turns solid again before it reaches the bottom. Name the change of state happening at each of these two places, and state for each whether the spacing between the wax particles increases or decreases.
hints: Write down the starting state and the finishing state at each place before you reach for a name.
Two of the five named changes in this lesson are exact reverses of each other: one needs energy to be supplied, the other needs energy to be removed.
For almost every substance, including wax, the particles in the liquid are slightly further apart than in the solid, because the regular close-packed arrangement has been lost.
guided_exercises.answer: Close to the flame the solid wax melts (solid to liquid), so the spacing between the wax particles increases slightly. On the cooler side of the candle the liquid wax freezes, also called solidifying (liquid to solid), so the spacing decreases again.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
Melting needs energy to be supplied. The wax near the flame absorbs energy, its particles vibrate more and more energetically, and eventually they have enough energy to overcome enough of the attraction holding them in fixed positions; the regular arrangement collapses into the liquid's disordered, mobile one and the particles end up slightly further apart.

Running down the cooler side of the candle, the liquid wax loses energy to the surrounding air. Its particles move less and less energetically until attraction pulls them back into fixed, ordered positions. This is freezing, the exact reverse of melting, and the spacing between the particles decreases again.

The wax is the same wax at every stage: only the arrangement, the spacing and the motion of its particles have changed.
common_errors: Thinking that freezing has to involve ice or a temperature below 0°C — freezing simply means liquid to solid, and candle wax freezes at a temperature well above room temperature.

guided_exercises.statement: Two identical open dishes of water are placed side by side: one at 20°C room temperature, one gently warmed to 60°C but well below boiling. Both lose water to the air only by evaporation. Predict which dish loses water faster, and explain why using particle energy.
hints: Both processes are evaporation, not boiling, since neither reaches 100°C.
Higher temperature means more energetic average particle motion.
More particles with enough energy to escape the surface means faster evaporation.
guided_exercises.full_solution: Both dishes evaporate because neither reaches the boiling point, but the warmer dish's particles have more energetic average motion. A larger proportion of its surface particles therefore have enough energy to escape the liquid's attraction at any given moment, so evaporation proceeds faster in the 60°C dish.
common_errors: Saying the 60°C dish is 'boiling slowly' — a temperature below the boiling point can never produce boiling, however fast the evaporation; the process named depends on temperature and location, not on speed.

exercises.statement: State the name of the change of state, and whether particle spacing increases or decreases, for each: (a) liquid chocolate setting solid as it cools; (b) morning dew forming on grass from water vapour in the air; (c) a puddle of water on a warm pavement slowly disappearing into the air.
exercises.answer: (a) freezing, spacing decreases; (b) condensation, spacing decreases; (c) evaporation, spacing increases.
exercises.full_solution: (a) Liquid to solid is freezing; particles lose energy and pack into a fixed, ordered arrangement, so spacing decreases. (b) Gas to liquid is condensation; particles lose energy and come together, so spacing decreases. (c) Liquid to gas at the exposed surface, below the boiling point, is evaporation; particles gain enough energy to escape, so spacing increases.

exercises.statement: A student claims: 'When ice melts, the water particles turn into a completely new, different kind of particle, which is why liquid water behaves so differently from ice.' Identify what is scientifically wrong with this claim and correct it.
exercises.answer: Melting does not change the identity of the particles; it is a physical change in spacing, arrangement and motion only.
exercises.full_solution: The same water particles are present in ice and in liquid water. What changes is their arrangement (regular to disordered), their spacing (slightly closer in most solids, though water is an unusual exception) and their motion (vibrating about fixed positions to moving freely around one another). The very different behaviour of ice and liquid water comes from this rearrangement, not from any change in what the particles themselves are.

exercises.statement: A sealed container of steam is cooled steadily until it becomes liquid water. Explain this process in terms of what happens to the particles' energy and spacing, and state what does NOT happen to the number of particles present.
exercises.answer: The particles lose energy as the container cools, move less energetically on average, and attraction pulls them into the liquid's closer, disordered arrangement; the number of particles present does not change.
exercises.full_solution: Cooling removes energy from the sample; it does not remove particles. As the particles' average motion energy falls, the attraction between them becomes sufficient to pull them from the gas's widely spaced, free arrangement into the liquid's closer, disordered one. The same fixed number of particles is present as liquid water at the end as was present as steam at the start.

exercises.statement: Liquid nitrogen boils at -196°C at normal atmospheric pressure. A small amount is poured into an open dish in a room at about 20°C. It immediately bubbles vigorously and disappears within seconds, producing a visible fog. Explain, using the vocabulary from this lesson, why this counts as boiling rather than evaporation, even though it is happening in an ordinary warm room.
exercises.answer: This is boiling: bubbles of nitrogen gas form throughout the liquid, not just at its surface. The liquid nitrogen is already at its boiling point (−196°C), and the room around it is far hotter, so energy flows in fast enough to keep it boiling throughout the liquid rather than just evaporating from its surface.
exercises.full_solution: Boiling is defined by where it happens (throughout the liquid, with bubbles) and by temperature (at the liquid's boiling point for the surrounding pressure) — not by whether the surroundings 'feel' hot or cold to a person. The room at 20°C is enormously hotter than liquid nitrogen's boiling point of -196°C, so heat flows into the liquid extremely quickly from every direction, not just at the exposed surface. This rapid, whole-liquid energy transfer produces vigorous bubbling throughout the liquid — boiling — rather than the slow, surface-only process of evaporation. The visible fog is water vapour from the room air condensing in the intense cold just above the dish, a separate change of state from the nitrogen's own boiling.
common_errors: Assuming boiling can only happen at high numerical temperatures like 100°C — boiling is defined relative to the substance's OWN boiling point, which for liquid nitrogen is very low, not relative to a fixed 'hot' temperature.

exam_questions.statement: A pure substance is heated steadily while it melts. Explain, in terms of particle energy and attraction, why its temperature does not rise while melting is taking place, even though energy is continuously supplied.
exam_questions.answer: Temperature measures the average energy of particle motion. While melting is happening, the energy supplied is used to let particles overcome enough of the attraction holding them in the solid's fixed positions so they can rearrange into the liquid's disordered, mobile structure, rather than to increase their average motion energy further; once melting is complete, further energy increases motion energy again and temperature rises.
mark_scheme: States that temperature depends on (average) particle motion energy.
States that energy continues to be supplied throughout melting.
States that the energy is used to overcome (some of) the attractive forces between particles.
States that particles can then leave their fixed positions and move past one another (the regular arrangement breaks down); attraction is overcome only enough for this, not removed completely.
Links the constant temperature to the energy not increasing the particles' average motion (kinetic) energy until all the solid has melted.

exam_questions.statement: Explain the difference between evaporation and boiling, referring to where each happens and the temperature condition for each.
exam_questions.answer: Evaporation happens only at a liquid's surface and can occur at any temperature below the boiling point; boiling happens throughout the whole liquid, with bubbles of vapour forming inside it, and occurs only once the liquid reaches its boiling point at the surrounding pressure.
mark_scheme: States evaporation happens only at the surface.
States evaporation can occur below the boiling point / over a range of temperatures.
States boiling happens throughout the liquid (bubbles forming inside it).
States boiling occurs only at the boiling point (for the given pressure).

challenge_questions.statement:
**Extension (beyond the 0654 syllabus).** Solid carbon dioxide, known as 'dry ice', is stored at about -78°C. A block of it left out in a warm room disappears completely over a few hours, and a dense white fog spills over the edge of the container while it does so. No puddle of liquid is ever seen.

(a) Explain why none of the five changes of state named in this lesson describes what has happened to the carbon dioxide, and give the name used for a solid that turns directly into a gas.

(b) State whether the spacing between the carbon dioxide particles increases or decreases, and explain your answer using the particle model.

(c) Carbon dioxide gas is colourless, so the white fog cannot be the carbon dioxide itself. Name the change of state that produces the fog and state which substance it involves.
challenge_questions.answer: (a) Melting, freezing, boiling, evaporating and condensing all involve a liquid at one end of the change, and here there is no liquid stage at all; a solid turning directly into a gas is called sublimation. (b) The spacing increases sharply: the particles go from being closely packed in a fixed, ordered arrangement to being far apart and moving freely. (c) The fog is condensation: water vapour already present in the room air is cooled by the very cold carbon dioxide gas and condenses into a mist of tiny liquid water droplets.
challenge_questions.full_solution:
(a) Each of the five required names has a liquid at one end of it: melting and freezing connect solid and liquid, boiling, evaporating and condensing connect liquid and gas. The dry ice goes from solid straight to gas with no liquid stage at atmospheric pressure, so none of the five names fits. That direct solid-to-gas change is called sublimation. It behaves like melting and boiling happening in one step, so it is driven by energy entering the substance from the warm room.

(b) The carbon dioxide particles start closely packed in the regular, fixed arrangement of a solid and end up far apart, moving freely and randomly as a gas, so the spacing increases a great deal. The particles themselves are unchanged: the same carbon dioxide particles are still present, now spread through the room.

(c) The fog is water, not carbon dioxide. The carbon dioxide gas leaving the block is extremely cold, so the air just above the block is chilled well below the temperature of the rest of the room. Water vapour in that air condenses into a mist of tiny liquid droplets, which is what makes the fog visible. This is the same reason that the visible 'steam' above a kettle is a mist of droplets rather than water vapour itself.

Sublimation is worth knowing about, but note that it is not required by the 0654 syllabus: the physics content states that solid-to-gas and gas-to-solid changes are not examined.

mcq.stem: A kettle of water is heated. At 85°C, before any bubbles appear, water particles are already escaping from the surface into the air as water vapour. What process is this?

options.text: Boiling, because water is turning into gas.
options.why_wrong: boiling requires bubbles forming throughout the liquid at the boiling point; turning into gas alone does not distinguish the two processes.

options.text: Condensation, because vapour is appearing above the water.
options.why_wrong: vapour appearing above the surface as the water loses mass is liquid turning to gas, the reverse direction from condensation.

options.text: It cannot be either process until the water reaches exactly 100°C.
options.why_wrong: evaporation can happen at any temperature below the boiling point; it does not require reaching 100°C.

options.text: Evaporation, because it is happening only at the surface and below the boiling point.

mcq.explanation: surface-only vapour loss below the boiling point is the definition of evaporation, regardless of how close the temperature is to boiling.

mcq.stem: Which statement about attraction between particles in a liquid, formed by melting a solid, is correct?

options.text: Significant attraction remains between the liquid's particles; it is no longer enough to hold them in fixed positions, but it still holds the liquid together at a fixed volume.
All attraction between the particles has completely disappeared.
options.why_wrong: if attraction truly disappeared completely, the liquid could not keep a fixed volume at all, and would behave like a gas instead.

options.text: Attraction increases during melting, which is why the liquid can flow.
options.why_wrong: melting involves particles gaining enough energy to overcome attraction sufficiently to move past each other; attraction does not increase.

options.text: Attraction only exists in solids, never in liquids or gases.
options.why_wrong: this denies the liquid's observed fixed-volume behaviour, which depends on attraction still being significant.

mcq.explanation: a liquid keeps a fixed volume precisely because real attraction remains between its particles; melting overcomes enough attraction for mobility, not all of it.

mcq.stem: Which pair names two different processes that both go in the SAME direction, between the SAME two states?

options.text: Melting and evaporating
options.why_wrong: melting is solid to liquid; evaporating is liquid to gas — different pairs of states, not the same pair.

options.text: Boiling and evaporating
Freezing and condensing
options.why_wrong: freezing is liquid to solid; condensing is gas to liquid — different pairs of states, even though both are cooling processes.

options.text: Condensing and melting
options.why_wrong: condensing is gas to liquid; melting is solid to liquid — different pairs of states, not the same pair.

mcq.explanation: boiling and evaporating are both liquid-to-gas processes: the same pair of states in the same direction, distinguished only by location, temperature and rate, not by the states involved.

mcq.stem: A sealed flask of gas is cooled until some of it condenses into a liquid. What happens to the number of particles in the flask?

options.text: It decreases, because some particles are removed by the cooling.
options.why_wrong: cooling removes energy from particles, not particles themselves; the flask is sealed, so no particles can leave.

options.text: It increases, because liquid particles are smaller and more of them fit.
options.why_wrong: particles do not change size during a change of state, and no new particles are created.

options.text: It stays exactly the same; only the particles' energy and arrangement change.
It cannot be determined without knowing the substance.
options.why_wrong: the particle count in a sealed container is unaffected by any change of state, for any substance; no extra information is needed.

mcq.explanation: a sealed container keeps the same fixed number of particles throughout any change of state; cooling changes their energy and arrangement, never their number.

flashcards.front: Name the five changes of state covered in this lesson.
flashcards.back: Melting, freezing, boiling, evaporating and condensing.

flashcards.front: Give two differences between evaporation and boiling.
flashcards.back: Evaporation happens only at the liquid's surface and can occur below the boiling point; boiling happens throughout the liquid, with bubbles, only at the boiling point.

flashcards.front: True or false: attraction between particles completely disappears once a solid melts.
flashcards.back: False. Significant attraction remains in the liquid; melting overcomes enough of it for particles to move past one another, not all of it.

flashcards.front: What is condensation?
flashcards.back: The change of state from gas to liquid, as particles lose energy and attraction pulls them into a closer, disordered arrangement.

flashcards.front: Why does a puddle dry up on a warm day without ever boiling?
flashcards.back: Evaporation removes water particles from the surface at any temperature below the boiling point; boiling (100°C throughout) is not needed for the puddle to disappear.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Evaporation and boiling are the same process, just with different names.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Both processes turn a liquid into a gas, and everyday speech often uses 'evaporate' and 'boil' loosely for the same thing.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner says a puddle 'boils away' in the sun, or expects bubbles to form anywhere a liquid is losing mass to the air.
misconceptions.correct_model: Evaporation happens only at the liquid's surface and can occur at any temperature below the boiling point; boiling happens throughout the liquid, with bubbles of vapour forming inside it, and occurs only at the boiling point (at the surrounding pressure).
misconceptions.remediation: Compare a steaming mug of hot tea (evaporation, no bubbles, below 100°C) with a pan of water on a stove once bubbles appear throughout it (boiling, at 100°C).

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The attractions between particles disappear completely once a solid melts into a liquid.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Textbook wording that heating 'weakens' the attraction during melting can be read as the attraction switching off entirely rather than merely being overcome enough to let particles move past each other.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner says there is 'no attraction at all' between particles in a liquid, or expects a liquid's particles to fly apart like a gas's.
misconceptions.correct_model: Melting gives particles enough energy to move past one another and adopt a disordered arrangement, but significant attraction remains between them in the liquid — otherwise a liquid could not hold together at a fixed volume.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask why a liquid keeps a fixed volume at all if there were truly no attraction left between its particles, and contrast this with a gas, where attractions really are negligible.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A particle becomes a different kind of particle during melting, boiling, freezing or condensing.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Ice, liquid water and steam look and behave so differently that the change can seem like a change in the substance itself, not just its state.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner describes melting as water 'turning into a new substance' rather than the same particles rearranging.
misconceptions.correct_model: A change of state is a physical change: the same particles are rearranged, with no particles created, destroyed or converted into a different kind.
misconceptions.remediation: Trace one labelled particle through solid, liquid and gas drawings and confirm nothing about the particle itself is different in each drawing.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Cooling a substance works by removing some of its particles.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: A cooled gas sample can seem to 'vanish' into a smaller liquid volume, which invites the idea that material has been taken away rather than slowed down.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner explains condensation or freezing as particles 'disappearing' rather than losing energy and moving closer together.
misconceptions.correct_model: Cooling removes energy from the particles, not particles themselves; the same number of particles move less energetically and, if enough energy is removed, pack closer together in a more ordered arrangement.
misconceptions.remediation: Count particles before and after an imagined cooling step in a sealed container and confirm the number is unchanged.

common_mistakes.mistake: Calling any liquid-to-gas change 'boiling', including gentle surface vapour loss.
common_mistakes.why: Everyday speech often uses 'boiling' loosely for any visible loss of liquid to the air.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Check location (surface only, or throughout?) and temperature (below the boiling point, or at it?) before naming the process.

common_mistakes.mistake: Saying particle attraction disappears entirely in a liquid.
common_mistakes.why: A common textbook's phrase about attraction 'weakening' during melting can be over-read as attraction switching off.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Remember that a liquid keeps a fixed volume only because real attraction remains between its particles.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating a change of state as changing what substance is present.
common_mistakes.why: Ice, liquid water and steam look and behave very differently from one another.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Confirm the same particles are present before and after; only spacing, arrangement and motion change.

common_mistakes.mistake: Explaining cooling as removing particles rather than removing energy.
common_mistakes.why: A cooled gas occupying a smaller liquid volume can look as if material has vanished.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: In a sealed container, count particles before and after: the number never changes during any change of state.

exam_notes: When asked to explain a constant temperature during a change of state, say explicitly what the supplied energy IS being used for (overcoming attraction for rearrangement), not just that temperature 'stays the same'.
When distinguishing evaporation from boiling, answer with BOTH location and temperature condition — one alone is rarely enough for full marks.
Never write that particles 'change into' something else during a physical change of state; always describe rearrangement of the same particles.
A scenario using an unfamiliar substance (not water) is testing whether you apply the definitions correctly, not whether you know that substance's exact melting or boiling point.

summary.big_idea: Every change of state is a change in particle energy and attraction acting on the same unchanged particles, and the two liquid-to-gas processes are told apart by where and at what temperature they happen.
key_points: Melting, freezing, boiling, evaporating and condensing are five directions between the same three states, not five unrelated pieces of vocabulary.
During a change of state, supplied energy overcomes enough particle attraction for rearrangement, which is why temperature stays constant while the change is in progress.
Attraction between particles never disappears completely; a liquid's fixed volume depends on real attraction remaining.
Evaporation happens at the surface, at any temperature below the boiling point; boiling happens throughout the liquid, only at the boiling point.
A change of state never changes how many particles are present or what kind of particle they are.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Same particles, every time — a change of state moves energy and rearranges spacing; it never creates, destroys or converts a particle.
