prerequisites.statement: Read a value from a simple line graph by matching a position on one axis to the corresponding position on the other.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every exercise in this lesson starts from reading a time and a temperature off a graph before any particle reasoning begins.

prerequisites.statement: The ideas from the two previous lessons: the particle spacing, arrangement and motion of each state, and that energy transfer (not just temperature) drives a change of state.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: A curve section is read by combining a graph observation with the particle-energy explanation already built in the previous two lessons.

diagnostic_items.question: On a graph with time (minutes) on the horizontal axis and temperature (°C) on the vertical axis, the plotted line passes through the point where time = 12 and temperature = 45. What temperature does the graph show at 12 minutes?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: 45°C, read directly from the vertical axis value at the point where time = 12 minutes.

common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner reads the horizontal-axis value instead of the vertical-axis value as the temperature.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks that horizontal (time) and vertical (temperature) axis values are not confused before any heating-curve interpretation begins.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Practise reading two or three further points from a simple labelled line graph, always naming which axis each number comes from.

theory_blocks.title: Reading a heating curve section by section

assets.caption: A heating curve for a pure substance heated at a steady rate at constant pressure, from -10°C as a solid to 110°C as a gas. It melts at 20°C and boils at 80°C. Sloped sections are a single state warming; flat sections (plateaus) are changes of state at constant temperature.
assets.purpose: Give a concrete, fully labelled curve with readable plateau durations (4 minutes for melting, 20 minutes for boiling) to anchor the three-question reading routine.

theory_blocks.body:
A heating curve plots temperature (vertical axis) against time, or energy supplied at a steady rate (horizontal axis), for a substance heated at a constant rate and constant pressure. Sloped sections show a single state warming up: its particles' average motion energy, and so its temperature, is rising. [[blue:Flat sections — plateaus — mark a change of state]]: two states coexist throughout the plateau, and temperature stays constant even though heating continues.

In the curve shown, the substance starts as a solid at -10°C, warms to its melting point at 20°C, stays at 20°C for 4 minutes while it melts completely, warms as a liquid to 80°C, stays at 80°C for 20 minutes while it boils completely, then continues warming as a gas. The boiling plateau is much the longer of the two because separating the particles completely, as boiling does, needs several times as much energy as breaking up the solid's regular arrangement.

theory_blocks.title: Why the plateau is flat
theory_blocks.body:
Temperature measures the average energy of particle motion, not the total energy supplied so far. During a plateau, the heater keeps delivering energy at the same steady rate as before and after — nothing about the heat source changes. What changes is where that energy goes: instead of increasing the particles' average motion energy (which would raise temperature), it is used to overcome enough attraction between particles for them to rearrange into the next state's structure.

This is exactly why a plateau ends: once every particle present has finished rearranging (all the solid has melted, or all the liquid has boiled), there is no more rearranging left for the incoming energy to do, so it goes back into raising average motion energy and the temperature starts climbing again.

theory_blocks.title: Three questions for any section of a curve
theory_blocks.body:
For any specified section of a heating or cooling curve, three questions give a complete answer. **Which state or states are present?** A sloped section is a single state; a plateau is two coexisting states — name both. **Is the temperature changing?** Read this directly from whether the line is sloped or flat. **Where is energy transferring?** On a heating curve, energy is always entering, whether the section is sloped (temperature rising) or flat (state changing); on a cooling curve, energy is always leaving, whether sloped or flat.

Answering all three, every time, prevents the single most common error: describing only the temperature and leaving out which states are present or where the energy is going.

theory_blocks.title: A cooling curve is the same story, reversed

assets.caption: The cooling curve for the same substance, cooled at the same steady rate from 110°C to -10°C at constant pressure: the exact mirror image of the heating curve, with the same two plateau temperatures (80°C and 20°C) and the same two durations (20 minutes and 4 minutes).
assets.purpose: Show directly that a cooling curve never needs to rise to show energy leaving: both its sloped and flat sections already represent outgoing energy.

theory_blocks.body: Cooling the same substance at a steady rate, from gas back down to solid, produces a curve that falls (or stays flat) throughout — it never needs to rise to show that energy is leaving. A sloped section shows a single state cooling, with its particles' average motion energy decreasing. A plateau shows two coexisting states again — gas and liquid during condensation, or liquid and solid during freezing — with energy leaving the substance as particles lose enough energy for attraction to pull them into a more ordered arrangement, while temperature stays constant until that process is complete for every particle present.

keywords.definition: A graph of temperature against time (or energy supplied) for a substance heated at a steady rate and constant pressure.
A graph of temperature against time (or energy removed) for a substance cooled at a steady rate and constant pressure; the mirror image of its heating curve.
A flat section of a heating or cooling curve where temperature stays constant while a change of state takes place and two states coexist.

worked_examples.statement: **Reading the melting plateau.** Using the heating curve in this lesson, state the temperature of the melting plateau and how long it lasts.
knowns: The melting plateau runs from 3 minutes to 7 minutes, at a constant 20°C.
worked_examples.solution: The plateau sits at a constant 20°C. Its duration is $7-3=4$ minutes.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check by counting four separate one-minute intervals across the plateau: 3-4, 4-5, 5-6 and 6-7.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Reading the plateau's temperature as changing over its duration — a plateau is defined by temperature staying exactly constant throughout.

worked_examples.statement: **Applying the three questions.** Using the heating curve, answer the three-question routine for the section from 9 minutes to 13 minutes.
knowns: 9 to 13 minutes falls entirely within the sloped section from 7 to 15 minutes, where the substance warms as a liquid from 20°C to 80°C.
unknowns: States present, whether temperature is changing, and energy transfer direction.
worked_examples.solution: States present: liquid only (this section is sloped, not a plateau). Is temperature changing: yes, it is rising throughout this section. Energy transfer: entering the substance, increasing the liquid particles' average motion energy.
worked_examples.interpretation: All three answers are consistent with a single sloped section: one state, changing temperature, energy entering and raising motion energy.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Naming 'solid and liquid' for this section by assuming it is still part of the melting plateau — the melting plateau ends at 7 minutes; by 9 minutes melting is already complete and only liquid remains.

worked_examples.statement: **Explaining why the plateau has a fixed length.** Explain, in terms of energy, why the boiling plateau in this lesson's curve lasts exactly 20 minutes and not some other length of time.
knowns: The heater supplies energy at a constant rate throughout.
The plateau lasts from 15 to 35 minutes.
unknowns: Why the plateau has this particular, fixed duration.
reasoning: The plateau lasts exactly as long as it takes for every particle in the liquid sample to be supplied with enough energy to overcome attraction and join the gas.
Since the heater supplies energy at a constant rate, and the total energy needed to boil the whole sample is fixed by how much liquid is present, the time taken is fixed too.

Once the last particle has finished this rearrangement, there is no liquid left to boil, so incoming energy immediately starts raising the gas's average motion energy and temperature rises again — ending the plateau.
worked_examples.solution: The plateau's length is set by the total energy needed to boil the whole sample divided by the constant rate at which the heater supplies energy; with both of those fixed, the plateau's duration (20 minutes here) is fixed too, and it ends the instant the last of the liquid has finished boiling.
worked_examples.interpretation: A larger or smaller sample of the same substance, heated at the same rate, would show a longer or shorter plateau — the plateau's exact length is not a fixed property of the substance alone, but of the sample size and heating rate together.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Saying the plateau 'just happens to last 20 minutes' with no mechanism — the duration is a direct consequence of energy needed divided by energy supply rate, not an arbitrary graph feature.

worked_examples.statement: **Exam-style: a cooling curve section.** Using the cooling curve in this lesson, describe fully what is happening between 31 and 35 minutes.
knowns: 31 to 35 minutes is the freezing plateau, at a constant 20°C.
unknowns: A full three-question description of this section.
worked_examples.solution: States present: solid and liquid coexisting (this is the freezing plateau). Is temperature changing: no, it stays constant at 20°C throughout. Energy transfer: energy is leaving the substance continuously; it is being removed from the particles as attraction pulls them from the liquid's disordered arrangement into the solid's fixed, ordered one.
worked_examples.interpretation: Note that this is NOT the melting plateau from the heating curve, even though both sit at 20°C: here energy is leaving (freezing), not entering (melting), which the direction of the overall curve (falling, not rising) confirms.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Describing this section as 'nothing happening because temperature is constant' — states ARE changing (liquid becoming solid) and energy IS transferring (leaving), even though temperature itself stays fixed.

guided_exercises.statement: Using the heating curve, apply the three-question routine to the section from 36 to 38 minutes.
hints: Locate 36 to 38 minutes on the curve: is this section sloped or flat?
This section lies after the boiling plateau, which ends at 35 minutes.
A sloped section on a heating curve always has energy entering and raising temperature.
guided_exercises.answer: States present: gas only. Temperature: rising (from 90°C at 36 minutes to 110°C at 38 minutes). Energy transfer: entering, raising the gas particles' average motion energy.
guided_exercises.full_solution: By 36 minutes, the boiling plateau (which ends at 35 minutes) is already complete, so no liquid remains: the sample is entirely gas. The section is sloped, so temperature is rising, and energy is entering the substance and increasing the gas particles' average motion energy, exactly as in any single-state warming section.
common_errors: Naming 'liquid and gas' because the section is close to the boiling plateau on the graph — proximity on the time axis does not mean the plateau is still in progress; check the exact minute values given.

guided_exercises.statement: A student says: 'At 5 minutes on the heating curve, the substance is a liquid, because the temperature has already reached 20°C.' Identify the error and give the correct description of the state(s) present at 5 minutes.
hints: 5 minutes falls within the melting plateau, which runs from 3 to 7 minutes.
A plateau represents two states coexisting, not a single finished state.
Reaching the melting temperature does not mean melting is complete.
guided_exercises.answer: At 5 minutes, both solid and liquid are present together; melting is not yet complete.
guided_exercises.full_solution: The temperature reaching 20°C only marks the START of melting, not its completion. For the whole 4-minute plateau (3 to 7 minutes), solid and liquid coexist, with the fraction that is liquid increasing steadily from 3 to 7 minutes. Only once the plateau ends, at 7 minutes, has every particle finished melting, leaving liquid only.
common_errors: Assuming a plateau represents a single, already-changed state throughout — a plateau is exactly the region where two states are coexisting, not where the change has already finished.

guided_exercises.statement: Using the cooling curve, apply the three-question routine to the section from 24 to 30 minutes.
hints: Locate 24 to 30 minutes: this lies between the condensing plateau (ends at 23 minutes) and the freezing plateau (starts at 31 minutes).
A sloped section on a cooling curve always has energy leaving and temperature falling.
Only one state is present during a sloped section.
guided_exercises.answer: States present: liquid only. Temperature: falling (from just below 80°C down towards 20°C). Energy transfer: leaving the substance, decreasing the liquid particles' average motion energy.
guided_exercises.full_solution: By 24 minutes the condensing plateau has finished (it ends at 23 minutes), so the sample is entirely liquid; the next plateau (freezing) does not begin until 31 minutes. Throughout this sloped section, energy continuously leaves the substance and the liquid particles' average motion energy, and so the temperature, falls steadily.
common_errors: Expecting the cooling curve to rise at some point to show energy leaving — a cooling curve shows energy leaving throughout, by falling (single state) or staying flat (a change of state), never by rising.

exercises.statement: Using the heating curve, state (a) the melting point, (b) the boiling point, and (c) the duration of the boiling plateau, showing your subtraction.
exercises.full_solution: (a) and (b) are read directly from the temperature of each plateau. (c) The boiling plateau runs from 15 minutes to 35 minutes, so its duration is $35-15=20$ minutes; this can be checked against the time axis, where the plateau covers four of the five-minute intervals marked on it.

exercises.statement: A student argues: 'During the melting plateau, the particles must stop moving completely, because if they were still moving they would still be gaining energy and the temperature would rise.' Explain what is wrong with this reasoning.
exercises.answer: Particles keep moving throughout the plateau; it is their AVERAGE MOTION ENERGY, not their motion itself, that stays constant, because incoming energy is going into rearrangement instead.
exercises.full_solution: The error is treating 'particles are gaining energy' and 'temperature is rising' as the same statement. Particles ARE continuously receiving energy during the plateau — but that energy is used to overcome attraction and rearrange the particles' positions, not to speed up their average motion. Since temperature measures only average motion energy, it can stay constant even while particles keep moving and keep receiving energy.

exercises.statement: Using the cooling curve, apply the three-question routine to the section from 0 to 3 minutes.
exercises.answer: States present: gas only. Temperature: falling (from 110°C to 80°C). Energy transfer: leaving the substance, decreasing the gas particles' average motion energy.
exercises.full_solution: This section is sloped and occurs before the first (condensing) plateau, which begins at 3 minutes, so only gas is present. Energy leaves the substance throughout, and the gas particles' average motion energy — and so the temperature — falls from 110°C to 80°C by 3 minutes, at which point condensation begins.

exercises.statement: A different pure substance, with a melting point of 15°C and a boiling point of 200°C, is heated at a steady rate from -10°C to 220°C at constant pressure. Sketch, in words, the general shape of its heating curve, describing how many sloped sections and how many plateaus it would show and what each would represent.
exercises.answer: Three sloped sections (solid warming, liquid warming, gas warming) and two plateaus (melting at 15°C, boiling at 200°C) — the same overall pattern as the lesson's curve, just with this substance's own melting and boiling temperatures.
exercises.full_solution: Whatever the specific melting and boiling points, a pure substance heated steadily through all three states at constant pressure always shows the same general pattern: solid warms (sloped) from -10°C to 15°C; melts (flat plateau at 15°C); liquid warms (sloped) from 15°C to 200°C; boils (flat plateau at 200°C); gas warms (sloped) from 200°C to 220°C. The exact temperatures and plateau lengths differ between substances, but the sloped/flat/sloped/flat/sloped structure is general to any pure substance passing through all three states.
common_errors: Assuming every substance's heating curve must have the same numerical melting and boiling points as the lesson's example — only the STRUCTURE (three slopes, two plateaus) generalises; the specific temperatures are properties of each individual substance.

exam_questions.statement: Using the heating curve in this lesson, describe fully what is happening to the substance between 3 and 7 minutes. Your answer should state which state(s) are present, whether the temperature is changing, and where energy is transferring.
exam_questions.answer: Solid and liquid are both present together; the temperature stays constant at 20°C; energy continues to enter the substance and is used to overcome attraction and let particles rearrange from the solid into the liquid structure, rather than to raise temperature.
mark_scheme: States that both solid and liquid are present (coexisting), not a single state.
States that temperature stays constant (at 20°C) throughout this section.
States that energy continues to enter the substance during this section.
Links that entering energy to overcoming attraction / particle rearrangement rather than to raising temperature.

exam_questions.statement: Explain why a cooling curve never needs to rise in order to show that energy is leaving a substance, referring to both a sloped section and a plateau in your answer.
exam_questions.answer: Energy leaves the substance throughout a cooling curve, so the line falls or stays flat but never rises. In a sloped section a single state is cooling: the energy leaving comes from the particles' motion, so their average motion energy, and the temperature, decrease. In a plateau two states coexist (gas and liquid while condensing, or liquid and solid while freezing): the energy leaving is released as attraction pulls particles into a closer, more ordered arrangement, so their average motion energy stays the same and the temperature is constant until the whole sample has changed state; only then does the temperature fall again.
mark_scheme: States that energy is leaving throughout a cooling curve, in both sloped and flat sections.
Explains that a sloped section falls because average particle motion energy is decreasing.
Explains that during a plateau the energy leaving is released as particles are pulled by attraction into a more ordered arrangement, so average motion energy (temperature) does not fall.
States that a plateau shows two states coexisting (gas + liquid during condensing, or liquid + solid during freezing).
States that the temperature stays constant until the change of state is complete for the whole sample, and then falls again.

exam_questions.statement:
A boiling tube of molten stearic acid is taken out of a hot water bath and left to cool in the air. Its temperature is recorded every minute until the sample is solid. The graph below shows the results.

(a) Use the graph to state the freezing point of stearic acid. [1]

(b) State which state, or states, of stearic acid are present at 8 minutes. [1]

(c) Use the graph to find how long the sample takes to freeze completely. Show your working. [1]

(d) Explain why the temperature stays constant between 4 and 12 minutes, even though the sample is still losing energy to the cooler air around it. [2]
exam_questions.answer: (a) 70°C. (b) Solid and liquid are both present together. (c) The flat section runs from 4 minutes to 12 minutes, so freezing takes 12 - 4 = 8 minutes. (d) Energy continues to leave the sample throughout the flat section, but it is released as the attraction between particles pulls them from the liquid's disordered arrangement into the solid's fixed, ordered one. This release balances the energy lost to the air, so the particles' average motion energy, and therefore the temperature, does not fall until the whole sample has frozen.
mark_scheme: (a) Freezing point read from the flat section of the graph as 70°C.
(b) Names both states: solid and liquid present together at 8 minutes.
(c) Identifies the flat section as 4 minutes to 12 minutes and gives $12-4=8$ minutes.
(d) States that energy continues to leave the sample during the flat section.

(d) Links the constant temperature to energy being released as particles are pulled into the solid's fixed, ordered arrangement, so average particle motion energy does not fall until all the sample has frozen.

challenge_questions.statement:
A technician repeats the stearic acid cooling experiment with a second sample, which has been contaminated with a small amount of another substance. The second cooling curve has the same general shape, but its flat section is not truly flat: the temperature drifts slowly down from 66°C to 62°C instead of holding one value, and that section begins at a lower temperature than it did for the pure sample.

(a) State the freezing point of the pure stearic acid, and explain why no single freezing point can be quoted for the contaminated sample.

(b) Explain what this comparison tells you about using a sharp, flat plateau as evidence that a substance is pure.

(c) A third sample, labelled 'pure stearic acid', gives a cooling curve with a sharp flat section at exactly 70°C. State what this suggests about the sample, and give one reason why it is still not proof that the sample is stearic acid.
challenge_questions.answer: (a) The pure sample freezes at 70°C. The contaminated sample has no single freezing point because it freezes over a range, from 66°C down to 62°C, so there is no one temperature at which the whole sample turns solid. (b) A sharp, flat plateau at a single temperature is good evidence that a substance is pure; an impurity both lowers the freezing temperature and spreads the change over a range instead of a single value. (c) It suggests the sample is pure, because it froze sharply at a single temperature, and that this temperature matches pure stearic acid. It is not proof of identity, because another pure substance could happen to freeze at 70°C as well.
challenge_questions.full_solution:
(a) The pure sample's curve holds a constant 70°C from 4 minutes to 12 minutes, so 70°C is its freezing point. In the contaminated sample, the particles of the second substance get in the way of the stearic acid particles settling into their regular, ordered arrangement. Freezing therefore starts at a lower temperature and carries on over a range as the composition of the remaining liquid changes, so the curve drifts from 66°C to 62°C rather than holding one value.

(b) Two separate pieces of evidence come out of the comparison. First, a pure substance freezes (and melts) at one sharp temperature, giving a genuinely flat plateau. Second, an impurity lowers that temperature and turns the plateau into a slow drift over a range. A sharp plateau is therefore good evidence of purity, and a sloping, lower 'plateau' is good evidence that something else is mixed in.

(c) A sharp flat section at exactly 70°C is consistent with a pure sample of stearic acid, and it is strong evidence that the sample is pure, since an impurity would have broadened and lowered the plateau. It does not prove the sample is stearic acid, though: freezing point tells you that the substance is pure and what its freezing point is, not what the substance is. Any other pure substance that happens to freeze at 70°C would give the same curve, so a second piece of evidence, such as a boiling point measurement, would be needed before the label could be trusted.

mcq.stem: A heating curve shows a flat plateau while the heater continues to supply energy at a steady rate. What is the best explanation?

options.text: The heater has switched off during the plateau.
options.why_wrong: the heater keeps supplying energy at the same steady rate throughout; if it had switched off, the temperature would not start rising again when the plateau ends.

options.text: The thermometer has stopped working accurately during the plateau.
options.why_wrong: the constant reading is a genuine physical result of the particle energy going into rearrangement, not an instrument fault.

options.text: All of the substance's particles have temporarily stopped moving.
options.why_wrong: particles keep moving throughout the plateau; only their average motion energy stays constant, not their motion itself.

options.text: The incoming energy is being used to overcome attraction and rearrange particles, not to increase their average motion energy.

mcq.explanation: a plateau occurs because continuing energy is redirected into overcoming attraction for rearrangement rather than into raising average particle motion energy.

mcq.stem: Which states are present partway through a melting plateau?

options.text: Solid and liquid together.
Solid only, since melting has not fully finished.
options.why_wrong: if only solid were present, the temperature would still be rising as the solid warms, not sitting flat on a plateau.

options.text: Liquid only, since the melting temperature has been reached.
options.why_wrong: reaching the melting temperature starts melting; it does not mean the whole sample has finished melting.

options.text: It cannot be determined from a temperature-time graph alone.
options.why_wrong: a plateau is specifically the signature of two coexisting states on a temperature-time graph; this can be determined from the graph.

mcq.explanation: a plateau represents solid and liquid coexisting throughout its full duration, not a single state at either end.

mcq.stem: Which statement about a cooling curve is correct?

options.text: The line must rise briefly during each plateau to show energy escaping.
options.why_wrong: a cooling-curve plateau stays flat, not rising; the energy leaving during a plateau is released as particles are pulled into a more ordered arrangement, so the temperature stays constant rather than rising.

options.text: Both its sloped and its flat sections represent energy leaving the substance; the line never needs to rise.
Only the sloped sections represent energy leaving; the plateaus represent no energy transfer.
options.why_wrong: energy continues to leave during a plateau too — it is released as attraction pulls particles into a more ordered arrangement, so their average motion energy (and the temperature) does not fall until the change of state is complete.

options.text: A cooling curve is unrelated to the heating curve of the same substance.
options.why_wrong: a cooling curve for the same substance under the same conditions is the mirror image of its heating curve, with the same plateau temperatures and durations.

mcq.explanation: every section of a cooling curve, sloped or flat, represents energy leaving the substance; a falling or constant line is sufficient, and a rise is never needed.

mcq.stem: On the heating curve in this lesson, which section shows liquid only, with temperature rising?

options.text: 3 to 7 minutes.
options.why_wrong: this is the melting plateau: solid and liquid coexist and temperature is constant, not rising.

options.text: 15 to 35 minutes.
options.why_wrong: this is the boiling plateau: liquid and gas coexist and temperature is constant, not rising.

options.text: 7 to 15 minutes.
35 to 38 minutes.
options.why_wrong: by this section melting and boiling are both complete; the substance is gas only, not liquid.

mcq.explanation: 7 to 15 minutes is the sloped section after melting is complete and before boiling begins, so it shows liquid only with rising temperature.

flashcards.front: What do the two axes of a heating curve usually show?
flashcards.back: Temperature on the vertical axis; time (or energy supplied at a steady rate) on the horizontal axis.

flashcards.front: What does a flat 'plateau' on a heating or cooling curve represent?
flashcards.back: A change of state: two states coexisting, with temperature constant while energy continues to transfer.

flashcards.front: How does a cooling curve's shape compare with the heating curve of the same substance?
flashcards.back: It is the mirror image: the same plateau temperatures (and, if energy is removed at the same rate as it was supplied, the same plateau durations), but falling (or flat) throughout instead of rising (or flat).

flashcards.front: True or false: a plateau means the heater has switched off.
flashcards.back: False. The heater keeps supplying energy at the same rate; that energy goes into rearranging particles instead of raising temperature.

flashcards.front: True or false: a cooling curve must rise at some point to show energy leaving.
flashcards.back: False. Both falling and flat sections of a cooling curve represent energy leaving; it never needs to rise.

flashcards.front: What three questions should you answer for any section of a heating or cooling curve?
flashcards.back: Which state(s) are present? Is the temperature changing? Where is energy transferring (in or out)?

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A flat (plateau) section of a heating curve means the heater has switched off or stopped supplying energy.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: A flat line looks like 'nothing is happening', which learners naturally read as the heat source pausing.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner explains a plateau by saying 'the heating stopped' rather than describing where the continuing energy is going.
misconceptions.correct_model: The heater keeps supplying energy at the same steady rate throughout a plateau; that energy is being used to change the state of the substance (overcoming attraction for rearrangement) rather than to raise its temperature.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask what would happen to the length of the plateau if the heater really had switched off, versus what is actually observed (the plateau ends and temperature resumes rising).

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Particles stop moving during a plateau.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: A constant temperature can be misread as 'nothing changing at all', including particle motion.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner says particles 'pause' or 'freeze' during a plateau, rather than describing them as still moving while rearranging.
misconceptions.correct_model: Particles keep moving throughout a plateau; what stays constant is their average motion energy (hence temperature), while the incoming energy instead goes into overcoming attraction and changing the particles' arrangement.
misconceptions.remediation: Revisit the particle-energy explanation from the previous lesson and ask specifically what temperature does and does not measure.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A cooling curve has to rise at some point to show that energy is leaving the substance.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Learners sometimes expect 'losing energy' to look visually similar to 'gaining energy', rather than recognising that a falling and a flat line can both represent energy leaving.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner expects an upward bump on a cooling curve, or struggles to explain how a flat cooling-curve plateau still represents energy leaving.
misconceptions.correct_model: A cooling curve falls (or stays flat during a plateau) throughout; energy continuously leaves the substance, whether the line is sloping down (single state cooling) or flat (a change of state releasing energy as particles lose enough energy to adopt a more ordered arrangement).
misconceptions.remediation: Compare the heating and cooling curves for the same substance side by side and confirm every plateau and every slope has a mirror-image partner, with energy direction reversed but never a rise on the cooling curve.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A plateau always represents a substance in a single state.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: A single, unchanging temperature value can suggest a single, unchanging state, since both ideas involve 'nothing seeming to change'.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner names only one state (for example, 'it is a liquid') for a plateau that actually represents two states coexisting.
misconceptions.correct_model: A plateau represents TWO states coexisting at once — for example, solid and liquid together during melting — not a single unchanging state.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask what would be observed if a plateau were sampled halfway through: some solid remaining and some liquid already present, together.

common_mistakes.mistake: Explaining a plateau by saying the heater stopped working.
common_mistakes.why: A flat line looks like nothing is happening.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: State explicitly that energy keeps entering at the same rate, and say what it is being used for instead (rearrangement, not temperature rise).

common_mistakes.mistake: Naming only one state for a plateau.
common_mistakes.why: A single constant temperature value suggests a single, unchanging state.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always name BOTH coexisting states for any plateau, for example 'solid and liquid together', never just one.

common_mistakes.mistake: Expecting a cooling curve to rise to show energy leaving.
common_mistakes.why: Rising is intuitively linked to 'something happening', and falling or flat can both look like 'nothing happening'.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Remember that BOTH a falling slope and a flat plateau on a cooling curve represent energy leaving; a rise is never required.

common_mistakes.mistake: Describing a curve section using only the temperature, with no mention of states present or energy direction.
common_mistakes.why: Temperature is the easiest single value to read straight off the graph.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always answer the three-question routine in full: states present, is temperature changing, and where energy is transferring.

exam_notes: Always answer with all three parts: states present, whether temperature is changing, and the direction of energy transfer — a partial answer naming only one of these rarely earns full marks.
For a plateau, name BOTH coexisting states explicitly; 'it is changing state' alone is not specific enough.
State clearly that the heater (or cooling process) continues to act throughout a plateau; do not imply it pauses.
A graph question may specify an unfamiliar substance's melting and boiling points — apply the same slope/plateau structure and three-question routine regardless of the specific numbers given.

summary.big_idea: A heating or cooling curve's sloped sections show a single state's temperature changing; its flat plateaus show two states coexisting while energy still transfers, just not into temperature.
key_points: Sloped sections: one state present, temperature changing, energy transferring into (heating) or out of (cooling) particle motion energy.
Plateaus: two states coexisting, temperature constant, energy still transferring, but into (or out of) particle rearrangement instead.
A plateau's length is fixed by the energy needed for the whole sample to change state, divided by the constant rate of energy supply or removal.

A cooling curve is the mirror image of the heating curve for the same substance: the same plateau temperatures (and the same durations if energy is removed at the same rate as it was supplied), falling or flat instead of rising or flat.
Use three questions for any curve section: which state(s), is temperature changing, where is energy transferring.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: A flat line on a heating or cooling curve never means nothing is happening — it means two states are coexisting while energy transfers into or out of rearrangement, not temperature.

04_Gas_volume_temperature_and_pressure.j.title: Gas volume, temperature and pressure
04_Gas_volume_temperature_and_pressure.j.subject: Chemistry

objectives.statement: Describe qualitatively how a change of temperature can affect a gas's volume when pressure is held approximately constant.
Describe qualitatively how a change of external pressure can affect a gas's volume when temperature is held approximately constant.
Explain both effects using particle motion, spacing and collisions with the container walls.
Predict why heating a sealed, rigid vessel changes the gas's pressure rather than its fixed volume.

prerequisites.statement: In a gas, particles move freely and randomly, colliding with each other and with the walls of their container.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Gas pressure in this lesson is explained entirely as the result of particle collisions with the container wall.

prerequisites.statement: Heating increases the average energy of particle motion; cooling decreases it.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every temperature effect in this lesson is explained by linking temperature to how energetically gas particles move and collide.

diagnostic_items.question: A sealed box contains air. What are the air particles doing to the inside surface of the box, and what do we call the effect this has on the walls?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: The particles are moving freely and randomly, so they keep colliding with the inside surface of the walls. The combined effect of all those collisions on the walls is the gas pressure.

common_wrong_answers.answer: The particles sit still, or settle at the bottom, and only the ones at the bottom touch the box.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner does not yet picture gas particles in constant random motion striking every wall, so no collision explanation of pressure is available to build on.

common_wrong_answers.answer: The air presses on the walls because it is heavy.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner explains pressure by the weight of the gas rather than by particle collisions, so the lesson's mechanism will not connect to anything.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks the blocking prerequisite from an earlier lesson that gas particles move freely and randomly and collide with the container walls, before every pressure explanation in this lesson is built on it.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Go back to the gas diagram in an earlier lesson and ask the learner to trace one particle's path until it strikes a wall, then say what a million such strikes per second would feel like.

diagnostic_items.question: Two identical sealed flasks of air start at the same temperature. Flask A is warmed; flask B is cooled. In which flask are the air particles moving faster on average afterwards?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: Flask A. Heating increases the average energy of particle motion, so A's particles move faster on average; cooling decreases it, so B's particles move more slowly.

common_wrong_answers.answer: The same in both, because they are identical flasks containing the same air.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner does not yet link a temperature change to a change in how fast the particles move, which every temperature prediction in this lesson depends on.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks the blocking prerequisite from an earlier lesson that heating raises, and cooling lowers, the average energy of particle motion, before that link is used to predict volume and pressure changes.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Revisit the heating curve in an earlier lesson and ask what the rising sections of the curve say about how the particles are moving.

theory_blocks.title: Heating a gas in a flexible container

assets.caption: Left pair: a flexible piston lets the volume increase on heating, while the external pressure stays approximately constant; the dashed line marks the old piston level. Right pair: a rigid sealed vessel keeps the same volume when heated, so collisions become harder and more frequent instead, raising the pressure. The red arrows show particle motion: they are clearly longer in both 'after' panels because heating increases the average particle speed.
assets.purpose: Make the contrast between a flexible and a rigid container directly visible, with the same nine particles reused in both 'before' panels for a fair comparison.

theory_blocks.body:
In a container with a movable boundary — a syringe with a free plunger, or a balloon — heating the gas while the external pressure stays approximately constant makes its [[blue:volume increase]]. Cooling the gas the same way makes its volume decrease again.

Nothing is added to the gas and nothing is taken away: it ends up with exactly the same number of unchanged particles, simply spread through more space (or less). This description is all that Core requires; the particle explanation of *why* the boundary moves is Supplement, and is set out in the block 'Explaining the volume changes with particle collisions' below.

theory_blocks.title: Squeezing a gas at roughly constant temperature
theory_blocks.body:
Pushing on a movable boundary, such as a syringe plunger, at roughly constant temperature increases the external pressure on the gas and [[blue:decreases its volume]]. Reducing the external pressure instead — for example by pulling the plunger outward — lets the same gas occupy a larger volume.

Again the gas itself is unchanged: the same number of particles is squeezed into a smaller space, or allowed to spread through a larger one. The Supplement explanation in terms of collisions is given below.

Every prediction in this lesson names which variable is held approximately constant (temperature, or external pressure) and what kind of container is involved, because the outcome depends on both.

theory_blocks.title: Pressure is the result of collisions
theory_blocks.body: A gas's particles move freely and randomly, striking the walls of whatever contains them. Each individual collision pushes on the wall very briefly; the combined effect of enormous numbers of these collisions, every second, over the whole wall area, is what is felt and measured as [[blue:gas pressure]]. Anything that makes collisions happen harder or more often — faster average particle motion, or particles packed more closely together — increases the pressure a gas exerts on its container.

theory_blocks.title: Heating a gas in a rigid, sealed vessel
theory_blocks.body: A rigid, sealed vessel has walls that do not move, whatever pushes on them. Heating the gas inside still increases the particles' average speed and so the force and frequency of their wall collisions — but since the walls cannot move outward to relieve this, the volume stays exactly fixed and the pressure rises instead. The same mechanism (faster, more frequent collisions) produces a volume increase in a flexible container and a pressure increase in a rigid one; the difference is entirely about whether the boundary is free to move, not about anything different happening to the particles themselves.

theory_blocks.title: Explaining the volume changes with particle collisions
theory_blocks.body:
**Supplement only.** The two descriptions above are what Core requires; the explanation here is the Supplement objective 'explain, in terms of kinetic particle theory, the effects of temperature and pressure on the volume of a gas'.

**Heating at approximately constant external pressure.** As the particles gain average speed, their collisions with the movable boundary become harder and more frequent, pushing it outward. The boundary keeps moving until the gas's push on it is back in balance with the roughly unchanged external pressure, so the gas ends up occupying a larger volume at about the same pressure as before.

**Compressing at roughly constant temperature.** The same number of particles, moving at roughly the same average speed as before, is squeezed into a smaller space, so the particles collide with the walls more often. It is this increased [[blue:frequency]] of collision that balances the increased external push.

In both cases only the spacing of the particles and the force and frequency of their collisions change. The particles themselves never change in size, number or identity.

keywords.definition: The measurable, combined effect of very many gas particles colliding with a container wall every second.
A container whose walls cannot move, so its volume is fixed whatever happens to the gas inside.
A container boundary, such as a piston or balloon skin, that can move in response to a change in the balance between internal and external pressure.

worked_examples.statement: **A balloon in the sun.** A balloon containing 30 cm³ of air is left in direct sunlight. Its volume increases to 36 cm³, with the air pressure inside staying approximately the same as the air pressure outside throughout. Explain this increase using particle collisions, and state the percentage increase in volume.
knowns: Starting volume 30 cm³, final volume 36 cm³.
External (atmospheric) pressure stays approximately constant.
unknowns: Percentage increase in volume, and a particle explanation.
worked_examples.solution: $\dfrac{36-30}{30}\times100\%=\dfrac{6}{30}\times100\%=20\%$ increase. Sunlight warms the air, increasing the particles' average speed and so the force and frequency of their collisions with the stretchy balloon skin. The balloon skin is pushed outward until the gas's larger volume brings its internal push back into balance with the roughly unchanged outside pressure.
worked_examples.interpretation: The particle count inside the balloon has not changed; the same particles now occupy 20% more space because they are moving faster and colliding harder, not because any particle has grown.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Saying 'the air particles expanded in the heat' — the PARTICLES are unchanged; it is the SPACE between them, and so the balloon's volume, that has increased.

worked_examples.statement: **Pushing a syringe plunger.** A sealed syringe holds 40 cm³ of air at room temperature. The plunger is pushed in, at roughly the same temperature throughout, until the air occupies 25 cm³. Calculate the percentage decrease in volume and explain the result using particle collisions.
knowns: Starting volume 40 cm³, final volume 25 cm³.
Temperature stays roughly constant throughout.
unknowns: Percentage decrease, and a particle explanation.
worked_examples.solution: $\dfrac{40-25}{40}\times100\%=\dfrac{15}{40}\times100\%=37.5\%$ decrease. At roughly constant temperature, the particles' average speed is roughly unchanged, but pushing the plunger packs the same number of particles into a smaller space. Particles now collide with each other and with the syringe walls more often, and this increased collision frequency balances the increased push from the plunger.
worked_examples.interpretation: Temperature being held roughly constant is essential here: it isolates the effect of pressure/volume alone, without a simultaneous speed change complicating the explanation.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Explaining the volume decrease by saying the particles 'slowed down' — at constant temperature, average particle speed does not change; only particle spacing and collision frequency change.

worked_examples.statement: **Comparing two heated containers.** A syringe with a freely movable plunger and a sealed, rigid glass bottle each contain air at the same starting temperature and pressure. Both are heated by the same amount. Explain why the syringe's gas ends up at a larger volume but the bottle's gas ends up at a higher pressure, using the same underlying particle mechanism for both.
knowns: Both containers start at the same temperature and pressure.
Both are heated by an equal amount.
The syringe's boundary can move; the bottle's cannot.
unknowns: Why the two containers show different outcomes from the same cause.
reasoning: In both containers, heating increases the gas particles' average speed in exactly the same way, so both sets of particles collide with their walls harder and more often.

In the syringe, the plunger is free to move: it is pushed outward by the increased collisions until the gas's larger volume brings its push back into balance with the roughly unchanged external pressure.
In the bottle, the rigid walls cannot move at all, however hard or often particles strike them: there is no way for the volume to increase.
With volume unable to increase in the bottle, the increased force and frequency of collisions is measured instead as an increase in pressure.
worked_examples.solution: The same increase in particle speed and collision frequency occurs in both containers, because heating affects the gas particles identically in both cases. The outcome differs only because of what each container's boundary is free to do: a movable boundary (the syringe plunger) responds to increased collisions by moving outward, giving a larger volume at roughly the same pressure; a fixed, rigid boundary (the bottle) cannot move at all, so the same increased collisions are measured instead as a higher pressure at a fixed volume.
worked_examples.interpretation: This is the key idea of this lesson: a rigid container's gas does not fail to respond to heating — it responds with a pressure change instead of a volume change, for exactly the mechanical reason given above.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Saying the rigid bottle 'resists heating' or 'doesn't let the gas expand' as if the gas behaves differently inside it — the gas particles behave identically in both containers; only the WALL's ability to move differs.

guided_exercises.statement: A weather balloon, with a flexible skin, is released from the ground and rises into colder air higher in the atmosphere. If the external pressure around it happened to stay roughly constant over this rise, predict and explain what would happen to the balloon's volume as it cools.
hints: Cooling has the opposite effect on average particle speed to heating.
Slower, less frequent collisions push the flexible boundary with less force.
The boundary moves until balance with the external pressure is restored.
guided_exercises.full_solution: Cooling decreases the gas particles' average speed, so their collisions with the flexible balloon skin become less frequent and less forceful. With less outward push from inside, the external pressure (assumed roughly constant here) pushes the flexible skin inward until the gas's smaller volume brings the two pushes back into balance.
common_errors: Assuming a real weather balloon's volume change is caused ONLY by temperature — in practice external pressure also falls with altitude, which is a separate effect; this exercise specifically holds external pressure constant to isolate the temperature effect alone.

guided_exercises.statement: A sealed, rigid metal canister of gas is placed near a fire and warms considerably. State what happens to its volume and to its pressure, and explain both using particle collisions.
hints: Check the container type first: is the boundary free to move?
A rigid container's volume cannot change, whatever happens to the gas inside.
Decide where the extra collision force and frequency must show up instead.
guided_exercises.answer: The volume stays exactly fixed (the canister is rigid); the pressure increases.
guided_exercises.full_solution: Warming increases the gas particles' average speed, so their collisions with the canister walls become harder and more frequent. Because the canister is rigid and sealed, its walls cannot move outward to relieve this, so the volume cannot change; the increased force and frequency of collisions is instead measured as a pressure increase. (This is also why heating a sealed gas canister near a fire is dangerous: pressure can rise to a level the canister was not built to withstand.)
common_errors: Predicting the canister's volume will increase 'because gases expand when heated' — this general rule applies only when the container's boundary is free to move; a rigid, sealed canister's volume cannot change at all.

exercises.statement: A bicycle pump with the outlet blocked contains 50 cm³ of air. The handle is pushed in, at roughly constant temperature, until the air occupies 30 cm³. Calculate the percentage decrease in volume, and explain in particle terms why pushing the handle gets noticeably harder as the air is compressed further.
exercises.answer: $\dfrac{50-30}{50}\times100\%=40\%$ decrease. Pushing gets harder because the gas's pressure rises as it is compressed, so a greater force is needed to push the handle against that rising pressure.
exercises.full_solution: As the same number of air particles are packed into a smaller and smaller volume, they collide with the pump walls and the piston more and more frequently, which is a rising internal pressure. A larger external force on the handle is needed to keep compressing the gas against this rising pressure, which is why the pumping action feels progressively harder — nothing about any individual particle has changed; only their spacing and collision frequency have.

exercises.statement: A student claims: 'An aerosol can is dangerous near a fire because the gas inside expands and the can grows bigger until it bursts.' Identify the scientific error in this claim and give the corrected explanation.
exercises.answer: The can is rigid, so it does not grow bigger; the danger is a pressure increase, not a volume increase.
exercises.full_solution: An aerosol can is a rigid, sealed container, so its volume cannot increase, whatever the temperature. Heating increases the gas particles' average speed and so the force and frequency of their wall collisions; with the walls unable to move outward, this shows up entirely as a pressure increase. The can bursts because the rising internal pressure eventually exceeds what the rigid can was built to withstand — not because the can itself has expanded.

exercises.statement: For each scenario, state whether the GAS'S VOLUME increases, decreases or stays the same, and name the condition that is being held approximately constant: (a) a flexible balloon is cooled, with the outside pressure roughly unchanged; (b) a syringe plunger is pulled outward at roughly constant temperature; (c) a rigid sealed can is warmed slightly.
exercises.answer: (a) decreases, external pressure held roughly constant; (b) increases, temperature held roughly constant; (c) stays the same (volume is fixed by the rigid container), whatever happens to temperature.
exercises.full_solution: (a) Cooling reduces particle speed and collision force/frequency, so the flexible balloon's boundary is pushed inward by the roughly unchanged outside pressure until balance is restored at a smaller volume. (b) Pulling the plunger outward gives the same particles more space at roughly the same average speed, so they hit the walls less often and the gas pressure falls; the volume increases while the temperature stays roughly constant. (c) A rigid container's volume is fixed by definition; warming it changes pressure, not volume.

exercises.statement: A scuba diver's rigid metal air cylinder is filled at a dive shop and later left inside a car parked in direct sunlight on a hot day. Using particle collisions, predict and explain what happens to the pressure of the air inside the cylinder, and explain why manufacturers print a maximum safe storage temperature on cylinders like this.
exercises.answer: The cylinder's pressure rises as the car heats up; its volume cannot change because the cylinder is rigid and sealed.
exercises.full_solution: The cylinder is a rigid, sealed container, so its volume cannot increase whatever the temperature. As the hot car heats the air inside, the air particles' average speed increases, so they collide with the cylinder walls harder and more often; with the walls unable to move outward, this entirely shows up as a pressure increase. A maximum safe storage temperature is printed because, past a certain temperature, the resulting pressure could exceed what the cylinder was engineered to contain safely, risking a dangerous rupture — exactly the same mechanism as a sealed aerosol can overheating, applied to a new context.
common_errors: Predicting that the cylinder itself will expand or its volume will increase in the heat — a rigid metal cylinder's volume does not change meaningfully with temperature in this context; only its internal gas pressure responds.

exam_questions.statement: A sealed, rigid gas cylinder is warmed. Explain, using particle collisions, why its pressure rises even though its volume does not change.
exam_questions.answer: Warming increases the gas particles' average speed, so they collide with the cylinder's walls harder and more often; because the rigid walls cannot move outward to relieve this, the volume stays fixed and the increased collision force/frequency is measured as a rise in pressure.
mark_scheme: States that warming increases the gas particles' average speed (kinetic energy).
Links this to more frequent and/or more forceful collisions with the cylinder walls.
States that the rigid walls cannot move / volume is fixed.
Concludes that the unrelieved increase in collisions is measured as a pressure increase.

exam_questions.statement: A gas sample is held in a container with a freely movable boundary. Describe and explain, in terms of particles, what happens to its volume (i) when it is heated at roughly constant external pressure, and (ii) when the external pressure is increased at roughly constant temperature.
exam_questions.answer: (i) The volume increases, because faster, more frequent particle collisions push the boundary outward until balance with the roughly unchanged external pressure is restored. (ii) The volume decreases, because the boundary is pushed inward by the greater external pressure until the gas's smaller volume gives collisions frequent enough to balance it.
mark_scheme: (i) States that volume increases on heating.
(i) Links this to increased particle speed/collision force or frequency against the movable boundary.
(ii) States that volume decreases when external pressure increases.
(ii) Links this to the boundary being pushed inward until internal collision frequency balances the greater external pressure.

mcq.stem: A balloon's volume increases when the gas inside is heated, with outside pressure roughly unchanged. What best explains this?

options.text: Each gas particle physically grows larger when heated.
options.why_wrong: particles do not change size on heating; only their average speed and spacing change.

options.text: Heating creates new gas particles inside the balloon.
options.why_wrong: no new particles are created; the same fixed number of particles simply occupies more space.

options.text: Heating reduces the air pressure outside the balloon.
options.why_wrong: the scenario states external pressure stays roughly unchanged; the volume change comes from inside, not from an outside pressure drop.

options.text: Faster-moving particles collide with the balloon skin harder and more often, pushing it outward until the gas's larger volume rebalances the pressure.

mcq.explanation: increased collision force and frequency against a movable boundary is what pushes it outward until balance with the external pressure is restored at a larger volume.

mcq.stem: A sealed, rigid metal canister of gas is heated. What happens?

options.text: The pressure increases; the volume stays exactly fixed.
The volume increases; the pressure stays exactly fixed.
options.why_wrong: a rigid, sealed canister's walls cannot move, so its volume cannot increase whatever the temperature.

options.text: Both volume and pressure increase together.
options.why_wrong: volume cannot increase in a rigid container; only pressure can respond to the heating.

options.text: Neither changes, because the canister is sealed.
options.why_wrong: being sealed prevents gas escaping, not pressure changing; pressure still rises as particle collisions become harder and more frequent.

mcq.explanation: a rigid container's fixed walls cannot move, so heating shows up entirely as a pressure rise, with volume unchanged.

mcq.stem: A sealed syringe of gas is compressed at roughly constant temperature. What happens to the individual gas particles?

options.text: They are squashed into a smaller size.
options.why_wrong: compression changes the spacing between particles, never the size of an individual particle.

options.text: Their size and average speed stay the same; only the average distance between them decreases.
They slow down because they have less room to move.
options.why_wrong: at constant temperature, average particle speed does not change; less room changes spacing and collision frequency, not speed.

options.text: Some particles are destroyed to make room for the rest.
options.why_wrong: no particles are destroyed; the same fixed number simply occupies a smaller space.

mcq.explanation: at constant temperature, compression changes only the spacing between unchanged particles, not their size or average speed.

mcq.stem: What is the correct particle explanation for gas pressure on a container wall?

options.text: A single large gas particle pressing continuously on the wall.
options.why_wrong: a gas consists of very many small, separate particles, not one large one; pressure comes from their combined collisions.

options.text: An attractive force pulling the wall inward.
options.why_wrong: gas pressure pushes outward on the wall through collisions; it is not an attractive, inward-pulling force.

options.text: The combined effect of very many particle collisions with the wall, each pushing briefly, every second.
The weight of the gas resting on the bottom of the container.
options.why_wrong: pressure acts on every wall of the container, not only the bottom, and is produced by collisions, not by the gas 'resting' under gravity.

mcq.explanation: gas pressure is the measurable, combined effect of enormous numbers of brief particle collisions with the container wall every second.

flashcards.front: What produces gas pressure on a container wall?
flashcards.back: The combined force of very many particle collisions with the wall, every second.

flashcards.front: Heating a gas by the same amount in a flexible container versus a rigid sealed one: what differs in the outcome, and why?
flashcards.back: A flexible container's volume increases (pressure stays roughly constant); a rigid container's pressure increases (volume stays fixed) — same particle mechanism, different wall behaviour.

flashcards.front: True or false: heating always makes a gas's volume increase.
flashcards.back: False. It only increases volume if the container's boundary is free to move; in a rigid sealed container, heating raises pressure instead.

flashcards.front: At roughly constant temperature, what happens to a gas's pressure when its volume is reduced by compression?
flashcards.back: Pressure increases: the same particles collide with the walls more often in the smaller space.

flashcards.front: Why is heating a sealed aerosol can near a fire dangerous?
flashcards.back: The rigid can's volume cannot increase, so the heated gas's rising pressure can exceed what the can was built to withstand.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Individual gas particles physically expand (swell up) when the gas is heated.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: A heated gas sample visibly takes up more space, which can be misattributed to the particles themselves growing rather than spreading apart.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner says particles 'get bigger' or 'expand' when a gas is heated.
misconceptions.correct_model: Particles do not change size when heated. Heating increases their average speed and the frequency/force of their collisions with a movable boundary, pushing it outward until a larger volume is reached; the particles themselves are unchanged.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask what would need to be true of a SINGLE particle for 'the particle expands' to be correct, and contrast this with 'the same particle moves faster and pushes harder, more often'.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Any heated gas must increase in volume, even in a rigid, sealed container.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Learners generalise the common 'heating expands a gas' rule without checking whether the container actually allows expansion.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner predicts a rigid sealed bottle will increase in volume (or might burst from expanding gas) rather than describing a pressure increase.
misconceptions.correct_model: In a rigid, sealed container the volume cannot increase, whatever the temperature; heating instead increases the gas's pressure, because faster, more frequent particle collisions push against walls that do not move.
misconceptions.remediation: Compare a syringe with a free-moving plunger to a sealed glass bottle heated by the same amount, and ask what is different about each container's walls.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Compressing a gas crushes or squashes the particles themselves.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The visible shrinking of the gas sample as a whole is read as the particles themselves shrinking.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner describes compressed gas particles as 'squashed' or 'flattened'.
misconceptions.correct_model: Compression reduces the average distance between unchanged particles; it does not change the size or shape of any individual particle.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask what evidence would show a particle had actually been crushed, versus simply moved closer to its neighbours.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Pressure, volume and temperature can be compared between two situations without saying which one is being held constant.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: It feels natural to say 'heating increases volume' as a general rule without noticing that this is only true when pressure is free to stay roughly constant.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner predicts a volume or pressure change without stating what condition (temperature, pressure, or container rigidity) is being held fixed.
misconceptions.correct_model: Every comparison in this lesson states explicitly what is held approximately constant (temperature OR external pressure) and what kind of container is involved (flexible/movable boundary OR rigid, sealed), because the outcome depends on these conditions.
misconceptions.remediation: Before answering, write down which variable is fixed and which container type is involved; only then predict the outcome.

common_mistakes.mistake: Saying gas particles physically expand or grow when heated.
common_mistakes.why: The visibly larger occupied volume is wrongly attributed to the particles themselves growing.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: State explicitly that particle size never changes; only average speed and spacing change.

common_mistakes.mistake: Predicting that any heated gas must increase in volume, including in a rigid container.
common_mistakes.why: The common classroom example (balloons, syringes) always uses a flexible boundary, so the rule is over-generalised.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always check the container type first: a rigid, sealed container's volume cannot change, whatever the temperature.

common_mistakes.mistake: Describing compression as crushing or squashing the particles themselves.
common_mistakes.why: The visibly smaller occupied volume is wrongly attributed to smaller particles.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: State explicitly that compression changes only the spacing between unchanged particles.

common_mistakes.mistake: Predicting a volume or pressure outcome without stating which variable is held constant.
common_mistakes.why: It is easy to state a rule like 'heating increases volume' without noticing the hidden condition (constant pressure) it depends on.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always name explicitly what is being held approximately constant before predicting an outcome.

exam_notes: Always name the container type (flexible/movable boundary, or rigid/sealed) before predicting a volume or pressure outcome.
Always state explicitly which variable is being held approximately constant (temperature, or external pressure).
Explain pressure changes through collision FORCE and FREQUENCY, not through vague language like 'the gas pushes harder' without saying why.
Never write that a particle 'expands', 'shrinks' or 'is destroyed' — only spacing, speed and collision frequency change for gas particles in this topic.

summary.big_idea: Gas pressure is the combined effect of particle collisions with container walls; whether heating changes a gas's volume or its pressure depends entirely on whether the container's boundary is free to move.
key_points: Gas pressure on a wall is produced by the combined force of enormous numbers of brief particle collisions, every second.
Heating a gas in a flexible container, at roughly constant external pressure, increases its volume: faster collisions push a movable boundary outward.
Heating a gas in a rigid, sealed container increases its pressure instead, because the fixed walls cannot move to relieve the increased collisions.
Compressing a gas at roughly constant temperature decreases its volume: the same particles, at the same average speed, are packed closer together.
Particles never change size, number or identity in any of these processes; only their spacing, speed and collision frequency change.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: The same heating always speeds up gas particles the same way — whether the RESULT is a bigger volume or a higher pressure depends only on whether the container's walls can move.
