objectives.statement: Describe and explain diffusion as random-motion mixing that produces a net spread of particles from a higher to a lower concentration.
Use a particle diagram or observation to explain why mixing continues towards a more even distribution without any particle coming to rest.
Explain qualitatively why gas molecules with a lower relative molecular mass generally diffuse faster than ones with a higher relative molecular mass, under comparable conditions.
State the variables that must be comparable before a difference in diffusion rate can be attributed to relative molecular mass.

prerequisites.statement: Gas particles move freely and randomly in all directions, colliding with each other and with the walls of their container (from an earlier lesson, an earlier lesson).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Diffusion in this lesson is explained entirely through this same random particle motion, now applied to mixing rather than to pressure.

prerequisites.statement: Relative molecular mass (Mr) is the sum of the relative atomic masses of the atoms in a molecule's formula (for example, Mr of H₂O = 1 + 1 + 16 = 18).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Comparing how fast two gases diffuse in this lesson depends on being able to work out and compare their relative molecular masses.

diagnostic_items.question: Using relative atomic masses H = 1, C = 12, O = 16, calculate the relative molecular mass of carbon dioxide, CO₂.

common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner adds only one oxygen atom's mass (12 + 16) and forgets the formula shows two oxygen atoms.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Checks that relative molecular mass can be calculated correctly from a formula before it is used to compare diffusion rates.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Practise writing out each atom in the formula separately before adding, counting every atom shown by a subscript.

theory_blocks.title: Random motion, net spreading

assets.caption: The same 12 scent particles (filled), released on the left of a container that is already full of air particles (open circles). Random motion mixes the scent particles evenly among the air particles over time. Every particle keeps moving randomly throughout; no directed force or current is involved.
assets.purpose: Show diffusion as mixing, not as expansion into an empty space: the container holds air particles in both panels, and the scent particles go from concentrated on the left to evenly spread among them, with motion arrows pointing in many different directions even after spreading.

theory_blocks.body:
Diffusion is the spreading of particles from a region where they are more concentrated into a region where they are less concentrated, caused entirely by [[blue:each particle's own random motion]]. A familiar gas example is a scent spreading through still air: particles of the scent mix among the air particles already present, rather than being carried by any directed force.

Each individual particle moves randomly, in any direction, colliding frequently with other particles. There is no 'pull' towards the dilute region acting on any one particle. The net spread happens at the level of the whole population: with far more particles starting in the concentrated region, simple random motion in all directions means more particles move out of that region than move back into it, until the distribution becomes even.

theory_blocks.title: Even spread is not stillness
theory_blocks.body: Once a mixture's concentration looks the same everywhere, every particle is still moving exactly as randomly as before — nothing about an individual particle's motion has changed. What has changed is that, with concentration now equal throughout, the number of particles randomly crossing from region A to region B in any interval of time is balanced, on average, by the number randomly crossing the other way. This is a [[blue:**dynamic equilibrium**]]: constant motion with no further NET change in the observable distribution, not a state of rest.

theory_blocks.title: Why lighter molecules generally diffuse faster
theory_blocks.body:
At a given temperature, particles of different substances carry, on average, a comparable amount of kinetic energy. For a molecule with a smaller relative molecular mass to carry a comparable amount of energy, it must on average move faster than a molecule with a larger relative molecular mass. Since diffusion depends on how quickly individual particles move and collide their way through a mixture, a gas made of lower-Mr molecules generally diffuses faster than one made of higher-Mr molecules, under otherwise comparable conditions.

This comparison is kept strictly qualitative here: no square-root rate law or numerical diffusion-rate formula is required at this level, only the direction of the relationship (lower Mr, generally faster) and the reasoning behind it.

theory_blocks.title: What 'comparable conditions' means
theory_blocks.body: A difference in diffusion rate can only be attributed to relative molecular mass once every other relevant variable is controlled. At minimum: the same temperature (since temperature itself changes average particle speed, independent of mass); the same geometry/distance travelled (a shorter path finishes 'first' regardless of mass); and still air or an enclosed, draught-free setup (so that bulk air movement, such as a fan or an open window, cannot explain the result instead). A comparison that changes any of these alongside the molecular masses cannot isolate the effect of mass alone.

keywords.definition: The net spreading of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration, caused by their own random motion.
A state in which particles continue moving, with motion between regions balanced so that there is no further net change in the overall distribution.
The sum of the relative atomic masses of all the atoms shown in a molecule's formula.

worked_examples.statement: **One particle's path.** A single coloured particle is tracked from the moment it is released at the left-hand edge of a still, closed container. Describe the shape of its path, and explain how this is consistent with the population of particles spreading from left to right overall.
knowns: The particle moves randomly, colliding frequently.
The population as a whole spreads from a concentrated start on the left to an even distribution.
unknowns: The shape of one particle's own path, and why it is consistent with the overall spreading.
worked_examples.solution: The tracked particle's path is irregular and random: it changes direction at every collision, sometimes moving right, sometimes left, sometimes up or down, with no consistent direction towards the empty side of the container. This is fully consistent with the overall left-to-right spread, because that spread is a population-level effect: with far more particles starting on the left than the right, random motion in all directions still produces more particles moving right (out of the crowded region) than left (back into it) during the early stages, even though any single particle's own motion has no preferred direction at all.
worked_examples.interpretation: The key distinction is between what a SINGLE particle does (moves randomly, no preferred direction) and what the WHOLE POPULATION does (spreads from high to low concentration) — both are true at once, at different levels of description.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Describing the tracked particle's path as 'heading towards the empty side' — an individual particle's motion is random in direction; only the population shows a net direction of spread.

worked_examples.statement: **Calculating relative molecular mass.** Using relative atomic masses H = 1, N = 14, Cl = 35.5, calculate the relative molecular mass of ammonia (NH₃) and of hydrogen chloride (HCl), and state which would be expected to diffuse faster at the same temperature, assuming comparable conditions.
knowns: NH₃ contains one N atom and three H atoms.
HCl contains one H atom and one Cl atom.
unknowns: Mr of NH₃, Mr of HCl, and which diffuses faster.
worked_examples.solution: $M_r(\mathrm{NH_{3}}) = 14 + 3(1) = 17$. $M_r(\mathrm{HCl}) = 1 + 35.5 = 36.5$. Since $17 < 36.5$, ammonia has the lower relative molecular mass, so under comparable conditions at the same temperature, ammonia (NH₃) would be expected to diffuse faster than hydrogen chloride (HCl).
worked_examples.interpretation: This is the basis of the classic ammonia/hydrogen chloride diffusion-tube demonstration: a visible white ring of ammonium chloride forms closer to the hydrogen chloride end of the tube, because the lighter ammonia molecules travel further in the same time.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Forgetting to multiply the hydrogen count by its subscript in NH₃ (using $14+1=15$ instead of $14+3(1)=17$) — every atom shown by a formula's subscript must be counted separately.

worked_examples.statement: **Explaining the inverse relationship.** A student says: 'Heavier molecules must diffuse faster, because they have more mass and so more force behind them.' Explain why this reasoning is incorrect.
knowns: At a given temperature, particles of different substances carry a comparable amount of kinetic energy on average.
unknowns: Why greater mass does not lead to faster diffusion.
reasoning: Kinetic energy depends on both mass and speed together, not on mass alone.
At the same temperature, different gas molecules carry a broadly comparable amount of kinetic energy on average, regardless of their mass.
For a LARGER mass to carry the same amount of energy as a SMALLER mass, the larger-mass molecule must be moving more slowly, not faster.
Diffusion rate depends on how fast particles actually move and collide their way through a mixture, so the slower-moving, higher-mass molecules diffuse more slowly, not faster.
worked_examples.solution: The reasoning confuses mass with force or speed. At a given temperature, different molecules carry a broadly comparable amount of kinetic energy; since a larger mass needs a lower speed to carry the same energy as a smaller mass, higher-Mr molecules move more slowly on average and so generally diffuse more slowly than lower-Mr molecules, not faster.
worked_examples.interpretation: This is the precise reason the relationship is an INVERSE one (lower mass, faster diffusion), which is the opposite of the everyday intuition that 'heavier things hit harder and therefore go further/faster'.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Treating 'more mass' and 'more force' as if they automatically mean 'faster' — at a shared temperature, it is speed (inversely related to mass, for comparable energy) that determines diffusion rate, not mass or force alone.

worked_examples.statement: **Exam-style: spotting a flawed comparison.** Two gas jars are set up: Gas A (lower Mr) is released into a jar in a warm room, and Gas B (higher Mr) is released into an identical jar in a cold corridor. Gas A appears to diffuse further in the same time. Explain why this result cannot, by itself, be used to conclude that Gas A's lower relative molecular mass is the cause.
knowns: Gas A: lower Mr, warm room.
Gas B: higher Mr, cold corridor.
Gas A diffused further in the same time.
unknowns: Why Mr cannot be confidently identified as the cause of the difference.
worked_examples.solution: Temperature was not held constant between the two gas jars: the warm room would, on its own, make Gas A's molecules move faster and diffuse further, regardless of its molecular mass. Because Mr and temperature were both different between the two setups, the observed difference in diffusion distance could be due to either variable (or both), and the experiment cannot isolate the effect of molecular mass alone.
worked_examples.interpretation: A valid comparison would need to repeat the test with both gases at the SAME temperature, in identical, still, draught-free containers, changing only the gas (and so only Mr) between the two trials.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Accepting the result as evidence for the Mr claim simply because the Mr values differed in the 'expected' direction — a flawed comparison can appear to confirm a correct idea by coincidence; the flaw in the method is the issue, regardless of whether the conclusion happens to also be true.

guided_exercises.statement: A few drops of dye are placed gently at the bottom of a tall, still container of water, with no stirring. Over several hours, the colour spreads upward and outward until the water looks evenly coloured throughout. Explain this observation using the particle model, and state what is still true about the dye particles once the colour looks even.
hints: Identify this as diffusion: spreading from a concentrated region to a less concentrated one, with no stirring (no bulk movement).
Explain the spread in terms of random motion of dye particles among water particles.
Decide whether dye particles stop moving once the colour looks even, or keep moving.
guided_exercises.answer: The dye spreads by diffusion: random motion of dye particles among the water particles produces a net spread from the concentrated start to the whole container over time; once the colour looks even, the dye particles are still moving randomly, with no further net change in the overall distribution.
guided_exercises.full_solution: With no stirring, any spreading is caused purely by random particle motion, not bulk movement — exactly the definition of diffusion. Far more dye particles start near the bottom than elsewhere, so random motion in all directions produces more dye particles moving away from the concentrated start than back into it, until concentration becomes even throughout. Once the colour looks uniform, dye particles continue moving randomly in every direction; the appearance of stillness reflects a BALANCE of motion in all directions (a dynamic equilibrium), not an actual halt in particle motion.
common_errors: Saying the dye particles 'stop moving' once the colour is even — motion continues; only the NET change in the visible distribution stops.

guided_exercises.statement: Using relative atomic masses H = 1, O = 16, S = 32, calculate the relative molecular mass of hydrogen (H₂) and of sulfur dioxide (SO₂). State which gas would be expected to diffuse faster at the same temperature, and name one condition that would need to be controlled for this comparison to be valid.
hints: Add up the relative atomic masses for each formula, counting every atom shown by a subscript.
Lower relative molecular mass generally means faster diffusion at a shared temperature.
A valid comparison needs more than one variable controlled; name at least one (temperature, geometry, or still air).
guided_exercises.answer: $M_r(\mathrm{H_{2}})=2$; $M_r(\mathrm{SO_{2}})=32+16+16=64$. Hydrogen (lower Mr) would be expected to diffuse faster. The comparison needs, for example, the same temperature for both gases.
guided_exercises.full_solution: $M_r(\mathrm{H_{2}}) = 1+1 = 2$. $M_r(\mathrm{SO_{2}}) = 32 + 16 + 16 = 64$. Since $2 \ll 64$, hydrogen has the much lower relative molecular mass and would be expected to diffuse considerably faster under comparable conditions. For the comparison to be valid, both gases need to be tested at the same temperature (and ideally also the same container geometry and still, draught-free air), otherwise a difference in diffusion distance could be caused by a different variable instead of molecular mass.
common_errors: Giving only the Mr calculation without naming a control variable — the question specifically also asks what must be held comparable for the Mr comparison to be a valid explanation.

guided_exercises.statement: A student wants to show that a lower-Mr gas diffuses faster than a higher-Mr gas. They release the lower-Mr gas into a short, wide tube and the higher-Mr gas into a long, narrow tube, both at the same temperature. Identify the flaw in this experimental design.
hints: List everything that differs between the two trials, not just the gas.
Check whether tube geometry (length, width) could affect how far or fast a gas appears to spread.
A valid test changes only the variable being investigated.
guided_exercises.answer: The two tubes have different geometry (length and width), not just different gases, so any difference observed could be caused by the tube shape rather than by the difference in molecular mass.
guided_exercises.full_solution: A valid comparison must hold every variable constant except the one being tested. Here, temperature was controlled, but tube geometry was not: a short, wide tube and a long, narrow tube are not directly comparable, since geometry alone can affect how a gas's spread is observed, independent of molecular mass. The experiment should use identical tubes (same length and width) for both gases, changing only which gas is used.
common_errors: Focusing only on whether temperature was controlled and missing that geometry differs too — 'comparable conditions' means ALL relevant variables, not just temperature.

exercises.statement: A student says: 'Diffusion happens because particles are attracted towards empty space.' Identify the error in this statement and give the corrected explanation.
exercises.answer: There is no attraction towards empty space; diffusion is explained by random particle motion, with a net spread arising only because more particles start in the concentrated region.
exercises.full_solution: Diffusion does not involve any force pulling particles towards a region of lower concentration. Each particle moves randomly and independently; the net spread from a concentrated region to a less concentrated one is a population-level outcome of that random motion, not evidence of any directed attraction or force acting on individual particles.

exercises.statement: Using relative atomic masses C = 12, O = 16, calculate the relative molecular mass of carbon monoxide (CO) and of carbon dioxide (CO₂). State which gas would be expected to diffuse faster at the same temperature, under comparable conditions, and explain why using particle energy.
exercises.answer: $M_r(\mathrm{CO})=12+16=28$; $M_r(\mathrm{CO_{2}})=12+16+16=44$. Carbon monoxide, with the lower Mr, would be expected to diffuse faster.
exercises.full_solution: At the same temperature, CO and CO₂ molecules carry a broadly comparable amount of kinetic energy on average. Since CO has the smaller mass (28 compared with 44), it must on average be moving faster than CO₂ to carry a comparable amount of energy, so CO molecules diffuse faster under otherwise comparable conditions.

exercises.statement: A claim is made: 'Gas X diffused across a room faster than Gas Y, so Gas X must have the lower relative molecular mass.' List two conditions that would need to have been controlled for this conclusion to be reliable.
exercises.answer: Both gases must have been tested at the same temperature, and in the same (still, draught-free) room/geometry, with nothing else differing between the two trials.
exercises.full_solution: Diffusion rate depends on more than just Mr: it also depends on temperature (which independently changes particle speed) and on the geometry/conditions of the space (distance, obstacles, and whether the air is genuinely still rather than moved by a draught or fan). Unless these were the same for both gases, a faster spread for Gas X could be explained by a warmer room, a shorter distance, or air movement, rather than by its molecular mass.

exercises.statement: A helium-filled balloon (relative atomic mass of He = 4) is known to shrink and lose its 'float' within a day or two, noticeably faster than an identical balloon filled with ordinary air (made mostly of N₂, Mr = 28, and O₂, Mr = 32). Both balloons are made of the same rubber material and kept in the same room. Using ideas from this lesson, suggest why the helium escapes through the tiny gaps in the balloon material faster than the surrounding air molecules diffuse in.
exercises.answer: Helium (Mr = 4) has a much lower relative molecular/atomic mass than the nitrogen and oxygen molecules that make up air (Mr = 28 and 32), so at the same room temperature helium particles move faster on average and diffuse through the small gaps in the rubber more quickly than the heavier air molecules move in.
exercises.full_solution: The same temperature applies to both balloons (same room), and the material and gap size are identical (same balloon type), so this is a fair, comparable-conditions comparison. Helium's very low relative atomic mass (4) means that, to carry a comparable amount of kinetic energy to the much heavier N₂ and O₂ molecules (28 and 32) at the same temperature, helium particles must move substantially faster on average. This faster average motion lets helium particles escape through the tiny gaps in the rubber considerably faster than air molecules diffuse in to replace them, so the balloon shrinks and loses buoyancy within a day or two.
common_errors: Explaining the shrinkage only as 'helium leaks out' without connecting the RATE of escape to relative molecular mass and particle speed — the lesson's reasoning chain (lower Mr, comparable energy, higher average speed, faster diffusion) should be used explicitly, not just asserted.

exam_questions.statement: Explain, using the particle model, why a gas released in one corner of a still, sealed room eventually spreads to fill the whole room evenly, and why the particles do not come to rest once the spread is complete.
exam_questions.answer: Each gas particle moves randomly in all directions, colliding frequently; with far more particles starting in the concentrated corner, random motion produces more particles moving away from that corner than back into it, until concentration is even everywhere. Once even, particles continue moving randomly in every direction; this is a dynamic equilibrium in which motion in all directions balances out, not a state of rest.
mark_scheme: States that gas particles move randomly in all directions (not along a directed path).
Explains the net spread as a population-level consequence of this random motion (more particles leaving the concentrated region than entering it, at first).
States that particles keep moving after the spread is complete.
Describes the final state as a dynamic balance/equilibrium, not stillness.

exam_questions.statement: Using relative atomic masses H = 1, Cl = 35.5, Br = 80, calculate the relative molecular masses of hydrogen chloride (HCl) and hydrogen bromide (HBr), and explain which would be expected to diffuse faster at the same temperature. State one further condition, other than temperature, that would need to be the same for this comparison to be valid.
exam_questions.answer: $M_r(\mathrm{HCl})=1+35.5=36.5$; $M_r(\mathrm{HBr})=1+80=81$. HCl, with the lower Mr, would be expected to diffuse faster, because at the same temperature its molecules move faster on average than the heavier HBr molecules. Besides the same temperature, the comparison is valid only if, for example, both gases travel the same distance through identical tubes/containers, in still (draught-free) air.
mark_scheme: Correctly calculates Mr(HCl) = 36.5.
Correctly calculates Mr(HBr) = 81.
States that HCl (lower Mr) diffuses faster.
Explains this via average particle speed at a shared temperature (lower mass, comparable energy, faster average speed).
States one further condition other than temperature: same distance/identical tubes or containers, or still (draught-free) air.

challenge_questions.statement: A sealed glass tube has cotton wool soaked in concentrated ammonia solution at one end and cotton wool soaked in concentrated hydrochloric acid at the other end, both inserted at the same moment. A white ring of ammonium chloride forms inside the tube where the ammonia gas (NH₃, Mr = 17) and hydrogen chloride gas (HCl, Mr = 36.5) molecules meet and react. Using relative atomic masses H = 1, N = 14, Cl = 35.5, explain why the ring forms closer to the hydrochloric acid end of the tube rather than at the exact midpoint, and explain why this experiment is normally set up with the tube held still and horizontal.
challenge_questions.answer: The ring forms closer to the hydrochloric acid end because ammonia (lower Mr, 17) diffuses faster than hydrogen chloride (higher Mr, 36.5), travelling a greater distance in the same time; holding the tube still and horizontal avoids bulk air movement or convection currents that would move gas by a process other than diffusion.
challenge_questions.full_solution: At the same temperature, ammonia molecules (Mr = 17) move faster on average than hydrogen chloride molecules (Mr = 36.5), since both carry a comparable amount of kinetic energy on average and ammonia's lower mass requires a higher average speed to do so. Faster-moving ammonia molecules therefore travel further along the tube in the same amount of time than the slower hydrogen chloride molecules travelling from the other end, so the two gases meet and react closer to the hydrochloric acid end, not at the midpoint. The tube is held still and horizontal specifically so that the only transport mechanism at work is diffusion (random particle motion): any tilting or air movement could add convection or bulk flow, which would move gas by an entirely different process and make the distances no longer a fair test of relative molecular mass alone.

mcq.stem: A particle of scent gas is tracked individually after being released in one corner of a still room. What is the best description of its path?

options.text: A straight path heading directly away from the corner towards the most empty part of the room.
options.why_wrong: individual particles move randomly; only the population as a whole shows a net direction of spread, not any single particle.

options.text: A path that speeds up the further it gets from the corner.
options.why_wrong: nothing about the scenario changes an individual particle's average speed as it moves through the room; speed depends on temperature, not on distance from the release point.

options.text: A path that eventually stops once the particle reaches 'empty' space.
options.why_wrong: particles do not stop moving; random motion continues throughout, wherever the particle is in the room.

options.text: An irregular, random path, changing direction frequently, with no consistent direction towards the rest of the room.

mcq.explanation: any single particle's motion is random and undirected; the overall net spread is a separate, population-level pattern that emerges from many particles each moving this way.

mcq.stem: A dye has spread through a container of still water until the colour looks completely even. What is true of the dye particles at this point?

options.text: They continue moving randomly in every direction; motion into and out of any region is now balanced, on average.
They have stopped moving, since the colour is no longer changing.
options.why_wrong: particles keep moving randomly; it is only the NET, population-level change that has stopped, not individual motion.

options.text: They have bonded permanently to the surrounding water particles.
options.why_wrong: diffusion does not involve dye particles bonding to water particles; they remain separate, moving particles.

options.text: They now all move together in the same direction to stay evenly spread.
options.why_wrong: particles continue to move independently and randomly; there is no coordinated, same-direction motion maintaining the even spread.

mcq.explanation: an even distribution is a dynamic equilibrium: particles keep moving randomly, with motion between regions balanced rather than absent.

mcq.stem: At the same temperature, which gas would generally be expected to diffuse fastest: one with Mr = 2, one with Mr = 28, or one with Mr = 44?

options.text: The gas with Mr = 28.
options.why_wrong: this is not the lowest relative molecular mass of the three; the gas with Mr = 2 would be expected to diffuse faster still.

options.text: The gas with Mr = 2.
The gas with Mr = 44.
options.why_wrong: this is the highest relative molecular mass of the three, so under the inverse relationship it would be expected to diffuse slowest, not fastest.

options.text: All three diffuse at the same rate, because temperature is the same for all three.
options.why_wrong: temperature being equal is exactly what allows the comparison to isolate the effect of mass; it does not mean the rates are equal, since mass still differs between the three gases.

mcq.explanation: at a shared temperature, the lowest-Mr gas moves fastest on average and so generally diffuses fastest, consistent with the inverse relationship between Mr and diffusion rate.

mcq.stem: A fan is used to blow the scent of an air freshener across a classroom in a few seconds. Why is this NOT, by itself, good evidence for diffusion?

options.text: Fans cannot move scent molecules at all.
options.why_wrong: a fan clearly can move scent molecules; the issue is which process (bulk air movement vs random-motion diffusion) is responsible, not whether movement happens.

options.text: Scent molecules are too large to diffuse under any circumstances.
options.why_wrong: scent molecules do diffuse; the problem with this scenario is that the fan's bulk airflow is doing the work here, not that diffusion is impossible for these molecules.

options.text: The fan causes bulk movement of air, a different process from diffusion, which should instead be demonstrated with still air.
A few seconds is too short a time for any particle process to occur.
options.why_wrong: the issue is not the timescale but the mechanism: a fan-driven draught, not random particle motion, is responsible for the fast spread observed here.

mcq.explanation: a fan moves whole parcels of air together (bulk movement/convection), a different mechanism from diffusion; isolating diffusion specifically requires still, draught-free conditions.

mcq.stem: Two different gases are compared for diffusion rate, using identical, still tubes but DIFFERENT temperatures. Why can this comparison not reliably show the effect of relative molecular mass alone?

options.text: Relative molecular mass has no effect on diffusion rate at any temperature.
options.why_wrong: relative molecular mass does generally affect diffusion rate at a GIVEN temperature; the issue here is specifically that temperature was not held constant, not that Mr is irrelevant.

options.text: Identical tubes always produce identical diffusion rates regardless of the gas used.
options.why_wrong: identical tube geometry controls for one variable, but it does not make the gases diffuse at the same rate; Mr and temperature can still produce different rates.

options.text: Diffusion cannot be compared between two different gases under any conditions.
options.why_wrong: diffusion rates of different gases can be validly compared, but only once every other relevant variable (including temperature) is controlled.

options.text: Temperature independently affects average particle speed, so a faster result could be caused by the higher temperature rather than by a lower Mr.

mcq.explanation: with temperature left uncontrolled, any observed rate difference could be due to the temperature difference, the Mr difference, or both, so the effect of Mr alone cannot be isolated.

flashcards.front: What is diffusion?
flashcards.back: The net spreading of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration, caused by their own random motion.

flashcards.front: True or false: once a mixture looks evenly spread, its particles stop moving.
flashcards.back: False. Particles keep moving randomly; only the NET change in the overall distribution stops (a dynamic equilibrium).

flashcards.front: At the same temperature, which diffuses faster: a lower-Mr gas or a higher-Mr gas?
flashcards.back: The lower-Mr gas: its molecules move faster on average for a comparable amount of kinetic energy.

flashcards.front: Name three conditions that must be comparable before attributing a diffusion-rate difference to relative molecular mass.
flashcards.back: The same temperature, the same geometry/distance, and still (draught-free) air.

flashcards.front: Why is a fan blowing scent across a room not good evidence for diffusion?
flashcards.back: A fan causes bulk air movement, a different process from diffusion; demonstrating diffusion requires still air.

flashcards.front: How do you calculate a molecule's relative molecular mass (Mr)?
flashcards.back: Add the relative atomic masses of every atom shown in its formula, counting each atom's subscript separately (e.g. Mr(CO₂) = 12 + 16 + 16 = 44).

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Every individual particle travels in a straight line directly from the concentrated region to the dilute region.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The overall, observable spreading looks directional, so learners assume each particle's own path must also be directional.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner draws a single straight arrow from the source to the rest of the container for every particle.
misconceptions.correct_model: Each individual particle moves randomly, in any direction, colliding frequently; it is only the overall population — far more particles starting in the concentrated region than arriving from the dilute region at first — that produces a net spread from high to low concentration.
misconceptions.remediation: Track one single particle's random path on the diagram and contrast it with the population-level pattern shown by all the particles together.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Once a mixture looks evenly spread, the particles stop moving.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: An unchanging, uniform appearance is read as nothing happening any more, including no more particle motion.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner says mixing 'finishes' or particles 'settle down' once the distribution looks even.
misconceptions.correct_model: Particles keep moving randomly even once the distribution is even; movement in every direction continues, but because the concentration is now the same everywhere, there is no further NET change in the observable distribution — this is a dynamic, not a still, equilibrium.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask what would happen if you could track one particle after the mixture looks even: does it stop, or does it keep moving randomly like before?

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A gas with a greater relative molecular mass always diffuses faster at the same temperature.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Learners sometimes assume 'heavier/bigger' means 'more forceful and therefore faster', reversing the actual relationship.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner predicts the gas with the larger Mr value will diffuse faster, or shows no clear reasoning linking mass to speed.
misconceptions.correct_model: At the same temperature, gas molecules with a LOWER relative molecular mass move faster on average and so generally diffuse FASTER than molecules with a higher relative molecular mass — the relationship is inverse, not direct.
misconceptions.remediation: Compare two molecules of very different Mr at the same temperature and ask which would need less energy to reach a given speed.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A moving current of air, such as from a fan, is by itself sufficient evidence of molecular diffusion.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Both a fan-driven draught and diffusion can carry a smell across a room, so the two can look identical from the observer's point of view.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner cites a fan or an open window as 'proof' of diffusion without ruling out bulk air movement as an alternative explanation.
misconceptions.correct_model: A fan or draught moves whole parcels of air together in one direction (bulk movement), which is a different process from diffusion, where net spreading results purely from each particle's own independent random motion. Demonstrating diffusion specifically requires still air, so that bulk movement cannot be the explanation for any spreading observed.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask what would need to be true of the room's air (moving or still) to be confident that an observed spread is diffusion and not just a draught.

common_mistakes.mistake: Drawing every particle moving in a straight line from the concentrated region to the dilute region.
common_mistakes.why: The overall, population-level spread looks directional, so each particle's path is assumed to be directional too.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Draw individual particle paths as random and irregular; only the whole population shows a net direction.

common_mistakes.mistake: Saying particles stop moving once a mixture looks even.
common_mistakes.why: An unchanging appearance is read as no further particle activity.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Describe the even state as a dynamic equilibrium: particles still move randomly; only the net distribution stops changing.

common_mistakes.mistake: Predicting that a higher relative molecular mass means faster diffusion.
common_mistakes.why: Greater mass is intuitively associated with 'more force' and so, wrongly, with 'faster'.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Remember the relationship is inverse: at a shared temperature, lower Mr generally means faster diffusion, because lower-mass molecules move faster on average for a comparable amount of energy.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating a fan-driven draught or open window as proof of diffusion.
common_mistakes.why: Both a draught and diffusion can spread a smell across a room, and look identical to an observer.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Confirm the air was genuinely still before attributing any spreading specifically to diffusion rather than bulk air movement.

exam_notes: When explaining diffusion, always distinguish an individual particle's RANDOM motion from the POPULATION's NET spread — both must appear in a full-mark answer.

When comparing two gases' diffusion rates, state the Mr-speed-diffusion chain explicitly: lower Mr, comparable energy, higher average speed, faster diffusion — not just 'lower Mr diffuses faster' with no reasoning.
Always name the conditions (temperature, geometry, still air) that must be controlled before a diffusion-rate comparison is treated as evidence about molecular mass.
Never write that diffusion requires a fan, wind or other directed force; still, undisturbed conditions are what make diffusion identifiable.

summary.big_idea: Diffusion is the net, population-level spread that random individual particle motion produces, and — at a shared temperature and in comparable conditions — lower-mass molecules generally produce that spread faster.
key_points: Diffusion is a net spread from higher to lower concentration, caused entirely by particles' own random motion, not by any directed force.
An individual particle's path is random and undirected; only the whole population shows a net direction of spread.
Once a mixture looks even, particles keep moving randomly; this is a dynamic equilibrium, not stillness.
At the same temperature, lower-relative-molecular-mass gas molecules generally move faster on average and so diffuse faster than higher-Mr molecules.
A diffusion-rate comparison is only evidence about molecular mass once temperature, geometry and still air are all comparable between the two gases.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Diffusion is random individual motion producing a net population-level spread — and under a fair, controlled comparison, the lighter molecule generally gets there first.

summary.big_idea: Use the key chemistry ideas and methods from states of matter accurately in mixed practice and exam-style problems.

exercises.statement: When a metal such as copper is heated it expands. Explain what happens to the metal particles as the solid metal expands.
exercises.answer: The copper atoms themselves do not get bigger. They vibrate with greater amplitude about their fixed lattice positions, which increases the average distance between neighbouring particles, so the solid as a whole expands.
exercises.full_solution: In a solid, the particles are held in fixed average positions by strong forces of attraction and can only vibrate about those positions; they cannot move from place to place. When the copper is heated, the particles gain kinetic energy, so they vibrate faster and with a larger amplitude ('swing' further from their resting position). This pushes neighbouring particles slightly further apart on average, even though the regular arrangement (lattice) is maintained. Since every particle in the solid is, on average, slightly further from its neighbours, the overall volume of the block of copper increases — this is thermal expansion. The particles are not created, destroyed or changed in size; only their average spacing increases.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: (a) Draw diagrams to show the arrangement of particles in: (i) solid lead (ii) molten lead (iii) gaseous lead. (b) Explain how the particles move in these three states of matter. (c) Explain, using the kinetic theory, what happens to the particles in oxygen as it is cooled down.
exercises.answer: (a) Solid lead: particles shown as touching spheres in a regular, repeating pattern (a lattice), as in the supplied information. Molten (liquid) lead: particles shown close together but in an irregular, random arrangement, still touching/almost touching. Gaseous lead: particles shown as a few widely spaced spheres with large empty gaps between them. (b) Solid: particles only vibrate about fixed positions and do not change places with each other. Liquid: particles have some extra freedom — they can move around and slide past each other while staying close together, colliding frequently. Gas: particles move freely and rapidly in random, straight-line paths in all the space available, colliding with each other and the container walls much less often than in a liquid. (c) As oxygen gas is cooled its particles lose kinetic energy and slow down, so they collide less often and less energetically. At oxygen's boiling point (−183 °C, the supplied information) the particles are moving slowly enough for the (still fairly weak) forces of attraction between them to pull them together into contact: the gas condenses into liquid oxygen. On further cooling to oxygen's melting point (−218 °C), the particles no longer have enough energy to move around each other; they settle into fixed positions in a regular lattice and only vibrate — the liquid freezes into solid oxygen.

exercises.statement: Draw and label the graph you would expect to produce if water at 100 °C was allowed to cool to −5 °C.
exercises.answer: A cooling curve with three stages: (1) temperature falls steadily from 100 °C down to 0 °C as liquid water cools; (2) a flat, horizontal plateau at 0 °C while the water freezes into ice (temperature stays constant even though heat is still being lost, because the energy is being removed as latent heat of fusion rather than lowering the temperature); (3) temperature falls again, from 0 °C down to −5 °C, as the solid ice continues to cool. The x-axis is labelled 'time' and the y-axis 'temperature/°C', with the flat section at 0 °C labelled 'freezing point — water solidifies to ice'.
exercises.full_solution: This is a standard cooling-curve question built from the kinetic-theory ideas on melting/boiling points developed in the relevant theory (the supplied information gives water's melting point as 0 °C and boiling point as 100 °C). Starting at 100 °C, the liquid water loses heat to its surroundings and its temperature drops at a roughly steady rate (sloping line) because the particles are simply slowing down. Once the temperature reaches water's melting/freezing point, 0 °C, the graph flattens into a horizontal plateau: heat is still leaving the water, but this heat is supplied by the energy released as the particles form stronger attractions and lock into the fixed, ordered arrangement of ice, so the temperature does not fall — the temperature cannot drop below 0 °C until all the liquid has frozen. Only after freezing is complete does the temperature start falling again, now at a different rate (ice has a lower specific heat capacity than water, so its temperature usually falls more quickly) as the solid ice itself cools from 0 °C down to −5 °C. So the sketch should show: down-slope (100→0 °C) → flat plateau at 0 °C → down-slope again (0→−5 °C).
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: Ice on a car windscreen will disappear as you drive along, even without the heater on. Explain why this happens.
exercises.answer: Even though the ice is below 0 °C, some particles at its surface have enough energy to escape directly into the air as water vapour (a process like evaporation, but straight from a solid — sublimation). Driving along moves a continuous stream of air over the windscreen, which sweeps away the water-vapour particles as fast as they escape. This stops vapour building up next to the ice (which would otherwise slow further escape), so particles keep leaving the ice surface, and over time the ice gradually disappears without the temperature needing to rise above 0 °C.
exercises.full_solution: The kinetic theory explanation of evaporation given in the relevant theory — that at any temperature there is a spread of particle energies, and some particles at a liquid's surface have enough energy to escape as vapour even below the boiling point — applies here to the solid ice: a small fraction of the water particles at the ice's exposed surface have enough energy to break free directly into the air as water vapour, even though the bulk ice is well below 0 °C. Normally this escape would quickly slow down, because the air right next to the ice would become saturated with water vapour and particles would re-condense as fast as they left. Driving the car prevents this: moving air constantly replaces the air layer touching the windscreen, carrying the escaping vapour particles away before they can collide with the surface and stick again. With a fresh supply of 'drier' air continually passing over it, particles keep leaving the ice surface, so the ice slowly shrinks and eventually disappears, even with no extra heat supplied by the car's heater.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: When a jar of coffee is opened, people in all parts of the room soon notice the smell. Use the kinetic theory to explain how this happens.
exercises.answer: Particles responsible for the coffee's smell are gases that leave the surface of the coffee and move freely, rapidly and randomly in all directions through the air (diffusion). Because there are initially far more of these particles near the open jar than elsewhere in the room, there is a net overall movement of particles away from the jar into the surrounding air until, given enough time, they have spread out and mixed with the air particles throughout the whole room, reaching people in every part of it.
exercises.full_solution: This is a direct application of diffusion, explained using the kinetic theory in the relevant theory. Gas particles move constantly, rapidly and at random, colliding with one another and with the air particles already present in the room. There is no 'planning' to this movement, but because the smell-causing particles start out concentrated near the open jar (a region of high concentration) and the rest of the room has none (low concentration), random collisions mean that, on average, more of these particles move away from the jar than move back towards it. Over time this net movement — diffusion — spreads the particles out until they are evenly mixed throughout all the air in the room, which is why people everywhere eventually smell the coffee, even though no air currents were deliberately created to carry the smell to them.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: Describe, with the aid of diagrams, the diffusion of copper(II) sulfate solution.
exercises.answer: At the start, a small volume of concentrated blue copper(II) sulfate solution is carefully run into the bottom of a container of water, so there is a sharp boundary between the dense blue layer below and clear water above (like Figure C1.10a in this chapter, but with blue $\mathrm{CuSO_4}$ solution instead of green nickel(II) sulfate solution). Left undisturbed, the $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}$ ions move randomly through the water and gradually spread upward; the sharp boundary blurs and rises as blue colour appears higher in the container. After a long time (hours to days, since diffusion in liquids is slow), the ions become evenly distributed and the whole container is a uniform pale blue, with no visible boundary left (as in Figure C1.10b).
exercises.full_solution: This question mirrors the nickel(II) sulfate diffusion experiment shown in the supplied information of this chapter, just using copper(II) sulfate solution (blue) instead of nickel(II) sulfate solution (green). The solution describes the two diagrams the question calls for: Diagram 1 (start) shows a container with a layer of concentrated blue $\mathrm{CuSO_4}$ solution sitting below a layer of clear water, separated by a clearly visible, sharp horizontal boundary — the ions have not yet mixed. Diagram 2 (after enough time has passed) shows the whole container as one uniform pale blue colour with no boundary at all. The explanation behind the diagrams: the copper and sulfate ions in solution are in constant, random motion and gradually move from the region where they are concentrated (the bottom layer) into the region where there are none of them (the water above) — this net movement from high to low concentration is diffusion. Because the particles in a liquid are much closer together and collide far more often than in a gas, this process is noticeably slow, typically taking many hours or even days to reach a uniform colour throughout, unlike gas diffusion which can be seen within minutes.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: Explain why diffusion is faster in gases than in liquids.
exercises.answer: Gas particles are much further apart than liquid particles and experience only very weak forces of attraction between each other, so they can move rapidly in straight lines over large distances before colliding with another particle. Liquid particles are packed close together with significant forces of attraction between them, so they collide with their close neighbours extremely often, which limits how quickly they can spread into a new region. This is why gases diffuse to fill the available space far more quickly than liquids do.
exercises.full_solution: Diffusion speed depends on how freely particles can travel through the surrounding particles. In a gas, the particles are very far apart compared with their own size and the attractive forces between them are negligible, so between collisions each particle travels a relatively long distance ('mean free path') in a straight line, and this happens at high speed — this lets gas particles spread through an available space (like the whole of a room, as in the supplied information's bromine diffusion) within minutes. In a liquid, the particles are packed almost as closely as in a solid and still have significant forces of attraction holding them together, so a given particle collides with its many close neighbours extremely frequently and can only edge forward a very short distance between collisions (as seen in the supplied information, where the nickel(II) sulfate diffusion experiment takes days rather than minutes). Fewer, more free collisions in gases versus very frequent, hindered collisions in liquids is therefore the reason gas diffusion is so much faster than liquid diffusion.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: Are the following composed of atoms, molecules or ions? (a) carbon, C (b) water, $\mathrm{H_2O}$ (c) sodium chloride $\mathrm{Na^+Cl^-}$ (d) carbon dioxide, $\mathrm{CO_2}$ (e) iron, Fe
exercises.answer: (a) carbon, C — atoms. (b) water, $\mathrm{H_2O}$ — molecules. (c) sodium chloride, $\mathrm{Na^+Cl^-}$ — ions. (d) carbon dioxide, $\mathrm{CO_2}$ — molecules. (e) iron, Fe — atoms.
exercises.full_solution: The chemical shorthand given in each formula tells us which type of particle is involved, exactly as explained in this section of the chapter. (a) Carbon, written simply as the symbol C with no subscript or charge, is an element made of individual carbon atoms (in a giant structure), so the particles are atoms. (b) Water, H2O, is a covalent compound whose formula shows small groups of atoms (2 hydrogen atoms joined to 1 oxygen atom) bonded together — this is the definition of a molecule, so water is composed of molecules. (c) Sodium chloride is written with explicit + and − charges, Na+Cl-, which is the defining feature of an ionic compound: these charged particles are ions, held together by the attraction of opposite charges, not atoms or molecules. (d) Carbon dioxide, CO2, like water, is a covalent compound whose formula shows a small fixed group of atoms (1 carbon, 2 oxygen) joined together, so it too is composed of molecules. (e) Iron, written as the plain symbol Fe with no subscript or charge, is a metallic element made of individual iron atoms in a giant metallic structure, so — like carbon — it is composed of atoms.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: How would you use chemical shorthand to write a representation of the molecules of iodine and fluorine?
exercises.answer: Iodine is written as $\mathrm{I_2}$ and fluorine is written as $\mathrm{F_2}$, since both exist as diatomic molecules (two atoms of the element joined together).
exercises.full_solution: The relevant theory explains that several elements — hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, fluorine, chlorine, bromine and iodine — exist as diatomic molecules, i.e. their atoms are joined together in pairs rather than existing as single free atoms. Chemical shorthand represents this by writing the element's symbol with a subscript 2 to show that two atoms are joined in each molecule. Applying this rule: a molecule of iodine (symbol I) is written $\mathrm{I_2}$, and a molecule of fluorine (symbol F) is written $\mathrm{F_2}$. This is consistent with the supplied information in the same section, which shows a chlorine molecule as two chlorine atoms joined together and would be written $\mathrm{Cl_2}$ using the same convention.
